meta.blurb: The Moon probably began when a planet-sized object crashed into the young Earth. School may have skipped that part, and much more. Fifty short steps take you from the Big Bang to your own brain, and never talk down to you.
meta.bible:
You: the reader, who sat in a classroom and wants the parts that were left out. Voice: friendly, curious and plain, speaking to "you", never talking down. Every fact is real and rounded with "about"; where scientists are unsure, the text says so. The order runs from the whole Universe, to the Earth, to life, to atoms and energy, to the brain and how science works. chapters: A Planet, a Crash and a Moon

beats.scene: A student sits at a school desk by a window, a globe beside her
beats.summary: You remember school, and see that much was left out of the lessons.

beats.scene: A person stands in a dark field under a sky full of stars
beats.summary: A clear night sky shows a few thousand stars, all of them in our own galaxy.

beats.scene: The Moon hangs over a dark landscape with a thin ray of light
beats.summary: Moonlight takes a little over a second to reach us.

beats.scene: A bright Sun with a long beam of light reaching a small Earth
beats.summary: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth.

beats.scene: A beam of light crosses a dark space between two distant stars
beats.summary: A light year is the distance light travels in one year.

beats.scene: A tiny spacecraft passes a faint red star across a wide dark gap
beats.summary: The nearest star after the Sun is more than four light years away.

beats.scene: A telescope points at a faint spiral galaxy while a clock turns backwards
beats.summary: Looking far away means looking back in time.

beats.scene: A ring of countless galaxies around a small dot, with a question mark beyond
beats.summary: The part of the Universe we can see is about ninety billion light years across.

beats.scene: Countless galaxies of many shapes scattered across a dark sky
beats.summary: The visible Universe holds hundreds of billions of galaxies.

beats.scene: A winding path leads from the stars down to a human head
beats.summary: The book will move from the largest things to the smallest, and finally to the mind that asks.

beats.scene: Galaxies drift apart across a dark sky like dots on a stretching sheet
beats.summary: Galaxies are moving apart, so the Universe is expanding.

beats.scene: A film strip shows galaxies moving closer together frame by frame
beats.summary: If the Universe is expanding, it was once smaller, hotter and denser.

beats.scene: A tiny glowing point swells into a bright cloud against darkness
beats.summary: The Big Bang began nearly fourteen billion years ago.

beats.scene: Raisins in a rising loaf of dough move apart as it swells
beats.summary: The Big Bang happened everywhere as space stretched, so it has no centre.

beats.scene: A thick fog hides the start of a long road
beats.summary: Nobody knows what, if anything, came before the Big Bang.

beats.scene: A blazing white glow filled with tiny sparks fills the whole sky
beats.summary: In its first instant the Universe was incredibly hot and may have stretched very fast.

beats.scene: Tiny particles clump together in a hot glowing cloud
beats.summary: Within minutes the Universe made the centres of hydrogen and helium atoms.

beats.scene: A glowing orange fog fills space, then slowly clears
beats.summary: For about 380,000 years the Universe was a glowing fog, until atoms formed and light flew free.

beats.scene: A large radio antenna points at the sky as a faint hiss sounds
beats.summary: The first light still reaches us as a faint microwave glow, found by accident in 1965.

beats.scene: An old television full of grey static in a dark room
beats.summary: Three kinds of evidence support the Big Bang, including a little of old television static.

beats.scene: A dark space with faint clouds of gas and no stars yet
beats.summary: After the glow faded, a long dark age followed with no stars.

beats.scene: Gas gathers into a thick glowing ball as arrows point inward
beats.summary: Gravity pulled the thicker patches of gas together.

beats.scene: The first blue stars light up inside a dark cloud of gas
beats.summary: The first stars switched on perhaps a hundred million years after the Big Bang.

beats.scene: Inside a glowing ball, small atoms squeeze together into bigger ones with a flash
beats.summary: Inside a star, fusion joins hydrogen into helium and releases energy.

beats.scene: A star drawn as a ball, with arrows pushing out and pulling in
beats.summary: A star is a balance between gravity pulling in and heat pushing out.

beats.scene: A huge blue star beside a small red star, each with its own clock
beats.summary: Heavy stars burn fast and die young; small stars live for a very long time.

beats.scene: Layers like an onion glow inside a big star, each a different colour
beats.summary: Stars make carbon, oxygen and other elements from lighter atoms.

beats.scene: A giant star collapses and bursts into a brilliant cloud
beats.summary: When a giant star's core turns to iron, it collapses and explodes as a supernova.

beats.scene: Two tiny dense stars spiral together and burst into sparks of gold
beats.summary: Gold and other very heavy elements come from violent events, including colliding neutron stars.

beats.scene: A person's outline made of glowing stars and dust
beats.summary: Apart from hydrogen, most atoms in your body were made inside stars that died before the Sun was born.

beats.scene: Stars gather into a bright swirling island in the dark
beats.summary: Gravity gathered stars and gas into galaxies.

beats.scene: A spiral galaxy, a round glowing ball and a messy cloud side by side
beats.summary: Galaxies come in spiral, elliptical and irregular shapes.

beats.scene: A huge spiral galaxy from above, with the Sun marked far from the centre
beats.summary: The Milky Way holds hundreds of billions of stars and is about a hundred thousand light years across.

beats.scene: A small yellow dot circles a huge galaxy centre along a long curved path
beats.summary: The Sun goes around the galaxy once in about two hundred and thirty million years.

beats.scene: A pale band of stars arches across a dark night sky
beats.summary: The pale band of the Milky Way is our inside view of the galaxy's flat disc.

beats.scene: A black round hole bends the light of the stars around it
beats.summary: Black holes have gravity so strong that not even light escapes; one sits at the Milky Way's centre.

beats.scene: Two spiral galaxies drift toward each other across a dark space
beats.summary: The Milky Way and Andromeda may merge in several billion years.

beats.scene: A galaxy spins fast with a faint ghostly cloud around it
beats.summary: Galaxies spin too fast for their visible matter, so unseen dark matter must add gravity.

beats.scene: A chart of galaxies with arrows moving apart faster and faster
beats.summary: The expansion of the Universe is speeding up, and the unknown cause is called dark energy.

beats.scene: A pie chart of the Universe with a very thin slice of ordinary matter
beats.summary: Ordinary matter is only about five per cent of the Universe; the rest is dark matter and dark energy.

beats.scene: A swirling cloud of gas and dust shrinks around a bright centre
beats.summary: The Solar System began about four and a half billion years ago from a collapsing cloud.

beats.scene: A flat spinning disc of dust circles a new bright Sun
beats.summary: The spinning cloud flattened into a disc with the Sun in the middle.

beats.scene: Grains of dust stick into rocks that crash together and grow into small worlds
beats.summary: Dust stuck into pebbles, rocks and then planets.

beats.scene: Small rocky planets near the Sun and huge gas planets farther out
beats.summary: Rocky planets formed near the Sun, giant planets farther out where ice could form.

beats.scene: The Sun beside a tiny Earth for scale
beats.summary: The Sun is an ordinary star, more than a hundred times wider than Earth.

beats.scene: A small grey cratered planet beside a thick yellow cloud-wrapped planet
beats.summary: Mercury is a small baked world, and Venus is hottest because its thick air traps heat.

beats.scene: A red dusty plain with a dry river bed and a small rover
beats.summary: Mars is red from rust and once had rivers and lakes.

beats.scene: A giant striped planet with a huge red storm and small moons
beats.summary: Jupiter is the biggest planet, with a storm wider than Earth.

beats.scene: A planet with bright rings beside two blue ice giants
beats.summary: Saturn has rings of ice, and Uranus and Neptune are cold ice giants.

beats.scene: Icy comets and a small dwarf planet far from a distant tiny Sun
beats.summary: Beyond Neptune lie Pluto, icy bodies and comets.

beats.scene: A glowing red planet with seas of melted rock under a black sky
beats.summary: The young Earth was molten and had no ocean or solid ground.

beats.scene: Heavy metal sinks to the centre of a melted planet as rock floats
beats.summary: Heavy iron sank to the centre and lighter rock rose, forming layers.

beats.scene: A huge planet crashes into the young Earth with fire and sparks
beats.summary: A planet-sized object probably hit the young Earth and made the Moon.

beats.scene: An astronaut lifts a grey rock beside a lunar lander on a dusty plain
beats.summary: Moon rocks brought home by the Apollo astronauts resemble Earth's rocks, supporting the impact idea.

beats.scene: The Moon shows one face to the Earth as it circles
beats.summary: The Moon always shows us the same face.

beats.scene: Ocean water bulges toward the Moon while waves cover a beach
beats.summary: The Moon's gravity raises the tides.

beats.scene: The Moon on a long curved path drifting slowly away from the Earth
beats.summary: The Moon is moving away from the Earth by about four centimetres a year.

beats.scene: The tilted Earth turns steadily beside the Moon
beats.summary: The Moon probably helps keep the Earth's tilt steady.

beats.scene: A scientist holds up a rock beside a ticking clock
beats.summary: Radioactive decay lets scientists date rocks, and the Earth is about four and a half billion years old.

beats.scene: A tiny crystal glows under a microscope beside a map of Western Australia
beats.summary: The oldest known pieces of Earth are crystals nearly four and a half billion years old.

beats.scene: A cut-away of the Earth showing crust, mantle, outer core and inner core
beats.summary: The Earth has a thin crust, a thick mantle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.

beats.scene: Waves spread out from a rumbling point in the ground and cross the Earth
beats.summary: Earthquake waves reveal what is inside the Earth, including its liquid outer core.

beats.scene: A glowing ball of metal at the heart of the Earth
beats.summary: The inner core is solid and as hot as the Sun's surface; the moving outer core makes the magnetic field.

beats.scene: Hot rock rises and sinks slowly in a thick layer beneath the crust
beats.summary: The mantle is solid rock that flows very slowly.

beats.scene: A world map broken into large puzzle pieces with arrows
beats.summary: The crust is broken into plates that move a few centimetres a year.

beats.scene: Plates pulling apart, pushing together and sliding past in three scenes
beats.summary: Plates move apart, together or sideways, and the edges are where most earthquakes and volcanoes happen.

beats.scene: A crack opens in the ground beside a road, with a recorder needle jumping
beats.summary: Earthquakes happen when rock that has been stuck suddenly slips.

beats.scene: A volcano erupts above a ring of mountains around a wide ocean
beats.summary: Volcanoes form where melted rock reaches the surface, and many circle the Pacific in the Ring of Fire.

beats.scene: Two plates push together and a mountain range rises
beats.summary: Mountains rise where plates collide, and the Himalayas are still growing.

beats.scene: One great supercontinent slowly breaks apart into the continents of today
beats.summary: The continents were once joined as Pangaea; Wegener's idea of drifting continents was accepted only in the 1960s.

beats.scene: A thin blue band of air around the curve of the Earth
beats.summary: The air is mostly nitrogen, with about a fifth oxygen.

beats.scene: A thin shell of air around a planet beside a climber near a summit
beats.summary: The atmosphere is thin: half the air lies below about five and a half kilometres.

beats.scene: A wide blue ocean seen from above, with a comet streaking across the sky
beats.summary: Oceans cover most of the Earth, and where the water came from is debated.

beats.scene: Ice floats on a pond while fish swim below
beats.summary: Ice floats, so lakes freeze from the top and life survives beneath.

beats.scene: Clouds, rain and a river running back to a sea under the Sun
beats.summary: The Sun drives the water cycle, and the water you drink is very old.

beats.scene: Wind sweeps across a landscape as warm air rises from sunny ground
beats.summary: Uneven heating by the Sun makes the wind and the weather.

beats.scene: Sunlight enters through the air while warm rays are trapped under a thin blanket
beats.summary: The greenhouse effect keeps the Earth about thirty degrees warmer than it would be.

beats.scene: A forest, a coal seam and a power station chimney joined by arrows
beats.summary: Carbon cycles through air, life, oceans and rocks, and burning coal, oil and gas returns ancient carbon to the air.

beats.scene: A thermometer rising beside a graph line and a melting glacier
beats.summary: Carbon dioxide has risen from about 280 to over 420 parts per million, and the Earth has warmed by over one degree.

beats.scene: Scientists read air bubbles trapped in a long core of ice
beats.summary: Ice cores and other evidence show today's warming is caused by people.

beats.scene: Layers of coloured rock in a cliff with a fossil shell inside
beats.summary: Layers of rock and fossils record the history of the Earth.

beats.scene: A calendar of one year marked with the history of the Earth
beats.summary: If Earth's history were one year, people would arrive in the last forty minutes.

beats.scene: A single cell shaped like a tiny room with a question mark
beats.summary: Life is hard to define, but living things use energy, grow, reproduce and change over generations.

beats.scene: Sparks flash inside a glass flask of gas and water
beats.summary: In 1953 an experiment made amino acids from simple gases, showing that the building blocks of life form easily.

beats.scene: A hot spring and a deep-sea vent both glowing with warm water
beats.summary: Life may have begun in warm pools, deep-sea vents or on clay, but no idea is proved.

beats.scene: A layered mound of rock beside a shallow warm sea
beats.summary: The oldest signs of life are about three and a half billion years old.

beats.scene: A tiny round bubble with a thin skin holds glowing chemicals inside
beats.summary: A cell is chemicals inside a thin skin, and for billions of years all life was single cells.

beats.scene: A drop of water seen through a lens, with cells shaped like tiny rooms
beats.summary: All living things are made of cells, and a human body has about thirty-seven trillion.

beats.scene: A twisted ladder shape glowing inside a cell
beats.summary: DNA is a chemical code shaped like a twisted ladder, and its shape was worked out in 1953.

beats.scene: A mother, a father and a child standing in a line
beats.summary: Genes are stretches of DNA that code for proteins and pass from parents to children, with rare copying mistakes.

beats.scene: A small sailing ship at anchor beside a rocky island with strange animals
beats.summary: Charles Darwin sailed round the world on the Beagle from 1831 and noticed how living things differ from place to place.

beats.scene: Three panels show varied animals, a struggle, and the survivors with young
beats.summary: Natural selection: living things vary, some survive better, and helpful features are passed on.

beats.scene: Small birds with different beak shapes sit on a branch
beats.summary: Finches on the Galapagos Islands have beaks suited to their food, and scientists have watched beaks change within a few years.

beats.scene: A hospital bed beside a petri dish where a few bacteria survive
beats.summary: Bacteria evolve resistance to antibiotics, which is natural selection in action.

beats.scene: A wolf beside dogs of many shapes and sizes
beats.summary: People shaped dogs from wolves by choosing which animals bred, which is artificial selection.

beats.scene: A pea plant with yellow and green peas beside a monk in a garden
beats.summary: Gregor Mendel's pea experiments in the 1860s showed that features are passed on in separate units, now called genes.

beats.scene: A winding path with no goal at the end and many branches
beats.summary: Evolution has no goal or plan: mutations are random, but selection is not.

beats.scene: A fish with strong fins like small legs rests half out of shallow water
beats.summary: Fossils such as Tiktaalik, a fish with limb-like fins, show how groups of animals changed over time.

beats.scene: A family tree with branches ending in a fish, bird, mouse and person
beats.summary: DNA shows that all living things are related and share a common ancestor.

beats.scene: A student with a notebook holds a magnifying glass over a fossil
beats.summary: In science a theory is a well-tested explanation backed by many kinds of evidence.

beats.scene: Green-blue slime floats in a sunny sea with bubbles rising
beats.summary: Cyanobacteria use sunlight to make food and give off oxygen.

beats.scene: Red and grey striped rock beside a sea turning rusty
beats.summary: About two and a half billion years ago oxygen began to build up in the air.

beats.scene: A big cell swallows a smaller one that settles inside it
beats.summary: Complex cells probably arose when one cell took in another that became the mitochondria.

beats.scene: A string of small round cells joined together in a tiny ball
beats.summary: For about three billion years life stayed tiny; then cells began to live together as many-celled life.

beats.scene: Soft flat frond-shaped creatures lie on a quiet sea floor
beats.summary: The Ediacaran creatures lived about 570 to 540 million years ago and were soft and strange.

beats.scene: A sea floor crowded with strange animals with shells, spines and legs
beats.summary: In the Cambrian explosion, about 540 million years ago, most major animal groups appeared within a short span.

beats.scene: A strange spiny hunter with grasping arms swims past a trilobite
beats.summary: Eyes, hunters and trilobites appeared, and the Burgess Shale in Canada preserves them superbly.

beats.scene: A small jawless fish with a stiff spine swims in a dim sea
beats.summary: The first backboned animals, fish, appeared about 500 million years ago, and later fish grew jaws.

beats.scene: Green moss and tiny plants creep across bare grey rock beside a pool
beats.summary: Plants and fungi moved onto land about 470 million years ago and began to form soil.

beats.scene: Early insects crawl across a muddy shore beside a fish with strong fins
beats.summary: Small animals reached land first; later some fish became four-legged animals about 370 million years ago.

beats.scene: A steamy forest of giant ferns and trees with a huge dragonfly
beats.summary: Coal-forming forests and giant insects lived about 300 million years ago.

beats.scene: A barren orange landscape with erupting volcanoes and fading animals
beats.summary: About 252 million years ago the Great Dying killed most species, probably because of huge volcanic eruptions.

beats.scene: A timeline with five dark marks and new small creatures after each
beats.summary: There have been five major mass extinctions, each followed by recovery and new kinds of life.

beats.scene: A small two-legged reptile runs across a dry plain
beats.summary: Dinosaurs appeared about 230 million years ago as small, quick animals.

beats.scene: A huge long-necked dinosaur stands beside a small feathered dinosaur
beats.summary: Dinosaurs ranged from chicken-sized to heavier than ten elephants, and many had feathers.

beats.scene: A small feathered dinosaur beside an early bird and a modern sparrow
beats.summary: Birds are living dinosaurs, descended from small feathered meat-eating dinosaurs.

beats.scene: A huge Tyrannosaurus beside a Stegosaurus, with a tiny human outline far away
beats.summary: Tyrannosaurus lived closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus.

beats.scene: A long-necked swimming reptile in the sea and a winged reptile gliding above
beats.summary: Plesiosaurs, ichthyosaurs and pterosaurs lived in the seas and skies, but they were not dinosaurs.

beats.scene: A huge rock streaks across a dark sky toward a blue planet
beats.summary: About 66 million years ago an asteroid about ten kilometres wide hit Mexico.

beats.scene: A thin dark line of clay in a rock layer, with a scientist pointing
beats.summary: A layer of iridium-rich clay supports the asteroid impact; only the birds survived among the dinosaurs.

beats.scene: Small furry animals hide in burrows and grass while large animals move above
beats.summary: Small mammals lived beside the dinosaurs, and after the asteroid they survived and grew in size and kind.

beats.scene: A furry four-legged animal wades into a river beside a sleek early whale
beats.summary: Whales evolved from land animals, and fossils show their legs shrinking.

beats.scene: A grassy plain with a small early horse and monkeys in a tree
beats.summary: The first primates lived in trees, and as the world cooled, grasslands spread.

beats.scene: A chimpanzee beside a human, with arrows pointing back to a shared ancestor
beats.summary: Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor from about six or seven million years ago.

beats.scene: A small upright ape-like figure walks beside footprints in volcanic ash
beats.summary: Lucy, who lived about three million years ago, walked upright on two legs.

beats.scene: A hand holds a sharp stone flake beside a small fire
beats.summary: Early humans made stone tools from about two and a half million years ago and learned to use fire.

beats.scene: A line of tall early humans walks out of a green land
beats.summary: Homo erectus appeared nearly two million years ago and spread out of Africa.

beats.scene: Heavy-browed early people stand by a fire with a modern human in a cave
beats.summary: Neanderthals lived in Europe and Asia, and many people today carry a little of their DNA.

beats.scene: A group of modern humans stands on a grassy hill in Africa
beats.summary: Homo sapiens appeared in Africa about 300,000 years ago and later spread across the world.

beats.scene: A farm field, a village and a tall tower along a short ruler
beats.summary: Farming began about 11,000 years ago, and all written history is a tiny part of the story.

beats.scene: A microscope shows tiny bacteria on a fingertip beside a happy person
beats.summary: Microbes are everywhere, and the body holds about as many bacterial cells as human cells.

beats.scene: A stomach shape with friendly colourful bacteria inside
beats.summary: Most microbes are harmless or helpful, such as those in the gut that help digest food.

beats.scene: A scientist at a table with a flask of liquid and a microscope
beats.summary: In the 1800s Pasteur and Koch showed that germs cause many diseases.

beats.scene: A doctor washes his hands at a basin in an old hospital
beats.summary: In 1847 Semmelweis showed that washing hands saved the lives of mothers.

beats.scene: A doctor gently scratches a boy's arm with a thin needle
beats.summary: In 1796 Edward Jenner showed that cowpox protected against smallpox, and smallpox was wiped out by 1980.

beats.scene: Tiny defender cells learn a pattern shown on a harmless piece of germ
beats.summary: A vaccine trains the immune system to recognise a germ without making you ill.

beats.scene: A mould in a dish with a clear ring around it
beats.summary: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould killed bacteria, which led to penicillin and antibiotics.

beats.scene: A tiny spiky ball sticks to a large cell as copying starts inside
beats.summary: Viruses are tiny packages of genes that must use a living cell to copy themselves.

beats.scene: A hand pump in a London street with a map of dots around it
beats.summary: In 1854 John Snow traced a cholera outbreak to one pump, and clean water and sewers later saved many lives.

beats.scene: A rising graph line of human lifespan over two centuries beside a smiling family
beats.summary: Global life expectancy has more than doubled since 1800.

beats.scene: An ancient Greek thinker cuts a stone in half again and again
beats.summary: Ancient Greeks suggested that matter is made of atoms, meaning uncuttable pieces, but proof came much later.

beats.scene: A human hair beside a magnifying frame with rows of dots
beats.summary: An atom is incredibly small: a hair is about half a million atoms wide.

beats.scene: A tiny ball of dots with smaller dots circling it
beats.summary: Atoms have a nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons around it.

beats.scene: A big empty stadium with a grain of sand in the middle
beats.summary: Atoms are mostly empty space, as Rutherford found in 1911 using gold foil.

beats.scene: Rows of different coloured balls labelled with their number of protons
beats.summary: An element is a kind of atom, defined by the number of protons in its nucleus.

beats.scene: A big wall chart with rows of coloured squares that hold letters
beats.summary: The periodic table arranges the elements, and Mendeleev left gaps in 1869 that proved right.

beats.scene: Two small hydrogen atoms join one oxygen atom to make a drop of water
beats.summary: Atoms join into molecules, such as water, by sharing electrons.

beats.scene: A candle burns while smoke and heat rise from it
beats.summary: In a chemical reaction atoms are rearranged, never destroyed.

beats.scene: A glowing rock beside a counter that clicks
beats.summary: Some atoms are unstable and radioactive, which is useful for dating and medicine.

beats.scene: A leaf, a person and a star linked by arrows of tiny atoms
beats.summary: Atoms are never used up; they are recycled, and the atoms in you have been in other things before.

beats.scene: A ball rolling down a hill beside a lamp, a fire and a battery
beats.summary: Energy is the ability to make things change, and it exists in many forms.

beats.scene: A ball rolls down a slope while a warm glow rises from it
beats.summary: Energy is never created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another.

beats.scene: Tiny atoms jiggle faster in a hot cup than in a cold one
beats.summary: Heat is the jiggling motion of atoms, and the coldest possible temperature is about minus 273 degrees.

beats.scene: A hot cup of tea cooling beside a melting ice cube
beats.summary: Heat flows from hot to cold, and disorder tends to increase, which gives time its direction.

beats.scene: A bowl of porridge beside a running child with glowing cells
beats.summary: Food is chemical energy, which cells release using oxygen.

beats.scene: A hockey puck slides across ice while a heavy box refuses to move
beats.summary: Newton's first law: things keep doing what they are doing unless a force acts on them.

beats.scene: A person pushes a light trolley and a heavy trolley with the same push
beats.summary: Newton's second law: a bigger force changes motion more, and heavier things need more force.

beats.scene: A rocket lifts off with a stream of fire pushing down
beats.summary: Newton's third law: every force has an equal and opposite force, which is how rockets and swimmers move.

beats.scene: A skater glides along ice while a box scrapes across rough ground
beats.summary: Friction slows things down, but without it we could not walk.

beats.scene: The Sun above a tiny lump of matter beside a huge burst of light
beats.summary: Einstein showed that mass is stored energy, and the Sun turns about four million tonnes of matter into energy every second.

beats.scene: A pebble drops in a pond and ripples spread toward a small boat
beats.summary: Waves carry energy without carrying matter, and sound travels far slower than light.

beats.scene: A prism splits a ray of white light into a rainbow
beats.summary: White light is a mixture of colours, as Newton showed with a prism.

beats.scene: A ruler of waves from radio to gamma rays, with colours in one part
beats.summary: Visible light is a small part of a family of waves that includes radio, microwaves, X-rays and more.

beats.scene: A balloon sticks to a child's hair beside a small flash of lightning
beats.summary: Matter has positive and negative charges, and static electricity comes from electrons moving.

beats.scene: A battery joined by wires to a glowing bulb
beats.summary: An electric current is a flow of electrons through a circuit.

beats.scene: A compass needle points north above the Earth with curved field lines
beats.summary: The Earth acts as a giant magnet, which guides compasses and shields us from the Sun's particles.

beats.scene: A magnet moves in and out of a wire coil as a bulb lights
beats.summary: Moving a magnet near a coil makes electricity, which is how generators work.

beats.scene: A wave of electric and magnetic arrows moves across the page
beats.summary: Maxwell showed in the 1860s that light is a wave of electricity and magnetism.

beats.scene: A beam of light hits a metal plate and tiny particles fly off
beats.summary: Light also behaves like a stream of particles called photons, which solar panels use.

beats.scene: A city at night glowing with lights beside a power line
beats.summary: Electricity runs modern life, and about nine in ten people now have access to it.

beats.scene: An apple falls from a tree while the Moon circles above
beats.summary: Newton realised that the gravity that pulls an apple also holds the Moon in orbit.

beats.scene: An astronaut floats inside a space station above a blue Earth
beats.summary: Astronauts float because they are in free fall around the Earth, not because there is no gravity.

beats.scene: A small fridge magnet lifts a pin against the pull of the whole Earth
beats.summary: Gravity is the weakest of the four basic forces, but it adds up.

beats.scene: A heavy ball dents a stretched cloth while a small ball curves around it
beats.summary: Einstein's general relativity of 1915 says that mass bends space and time, and that is gravity.

beats.scene: Stars appear to shift beside the dark disc of the Sun during an eclipse
beats.summary: In 1919 an eclipse showed starlight bending around the Sun, as Einstein predicted.

beats.scene: A clock on a high mountain ticks slightly faster than one at sea level
beats.summary: Time runs a little slower where gravity is stronger, and GPS satellites must correct for it.

beats.scene: A rocket speeding past a beam of light that races far ahead
beats.summary: Nothing can travel faster than light, and fast-moving clocks tick slowly.

beats.scene: Two black holes spiral together, sending ripples across a starry sky
beats.summary: In 2015 gravitational waves from two merging black holes were detected, a century after Einstein predicted them.

beats.scene: A tiny particle shown as a wave and as a dot
beats.summary: Quantum physics: tiny things behave strangely, with energy in packets and limits on what can be known.

beats.scene: A computer chip, a laser beam and a phone beside a question mark
beats.summary: Quantum physics gives us lasers and chips, but it does not yet fit together with gravity.

beats.scene: A glowing outline of a head with sparks running along branched cells
beats.summary: The brain weighs about one and a half kilograms, has about 86 billion neurons and uses about a fifth of the body's energy.

beats.scene: A nerve cell with branches passes a spark to another across a tiny gap
beats.summary: Neurons send electrical pulses and pass chemical messages across gaps called synapses.

beats.scene: A web of glowing connections joining many cells
beats.summary: Each neuron connects to thousands of others, making at least a hundred trillion connections.

beats.scene: An eye looks at a tree while a brain paints it in colour
beats.summary: The brain builds the picture we see: the eye's image is upside down, and colour is made in the brain.

beats.scene: A diagram of a brain with labelled areas for seeing, moving, speaking and remembering
beats.summary: Different parts of the brain have different jobs, but they work together.

beats.scene: A person recalls a birthday party in a bubble above their head
beats.summary: Memories are spread across the brain, and recalling one rebuilds it, so memories can change.

beats.scene: A student reads a card beside a small calendar showing repeated review days
beats.summary: Learning strengthens connections, and reviewing after gaps works better than cramming.

beats.scene: A sleeping person in a dark room with a glowing brain above
beats.summary: The brain is busy during sleep, helping to sort memories, and most adults need seven to nine hours.

beats.scene: A child points at drawings and says a word while an adult smiles
beats.summary: Children learn speech by listening, and reading is a recent invention that borrows parts of the brain.

beats.scene: A glowing head with a question mark floating inside
beats.summary: Consciousness is still unexplained, and the link between brain and mind remains a mystery.

beats.scene: A child looks at a puddle with a question mark above
beats.summary: Science starts with curiosity and a question that can be tested.

beats.scene: A man measures the shadows of sticks in two far apart ancient cities
beats.summary: Eratosthenes measured the size of the Earth about 2,200 years ago using shadows.

beats.scene: Two plants, one in sun and one in shade, beside a ruler and notebook
beats.summary: A fair test changes only one thing at a time, tests a hypothesis and uses a control.

beats.scene: Two doctors look at a dish of bacteria beside a drawing of a stomach
beats.summary: Doctors once blamed stress for ulcers, but in the 1980s two doctors showed that a bacterium was the cause of many.

beats.scene: A scientist crosses out a wrong answer and writes a new one
beats.summary: Scientists try to prove their own ideas wrong, and being wrong is part of progress.

beats.scene: A loose cable plugged into a machine in a long tunnel
beats.summary: In 2011 scientists thought particles had moved faster than light, but the cause was a loose cable, and they said so.

beats.scene: A telescope and a pair of hands above an unfinished map
beats.summary: Science has limits: it cannot answer questions of values, and honest answers include that we do not know.

beats.scene: A blackboard list of open questions, with stars, cells and brains beside it
beats.summary: Big open questions remain: dark matter, the origin of life, consciousness and joining gravity with quantum physics.

beats.scene: A person stands in a field holding a handful of soil under the stars
beats.summary: You are made of stardust, and every part of this book connects to you.

beats.scene: A person looks up from a hill at the night sky, full of stars
beats.summary: You are part of the story, so keep asking questions.

A1A2: You sit in a classroom and wonder what the teacher left out.
In a dark place, you can see thousands of stars with your eyes.
Light from the Moon takes just over one second to reach you.
Sunlight takes about eight minutes to come to the Earth.
A light year is how far light goes in one year.
The next nearest star is more than four light years away.
When you look at far stars, you see the past.
The part of space that we can see is billions of light years wide.
Space holds hundreds of billions of galaxies, each full of stars.
This book starts with the biggest things and ends with you.
Far galaxies are all moving away from each other.
Long ago, everything was much closer together and very hot.
The Universe began nearly fourteen billion years ago.
The Big Bang did not happen in one place.
Nobody knows what came before the Big Bang.
At first, the Universe was hotter than anything today.
In a few minutes, small pieces joined to make the centres of atoms.
For a long time, the whole Universe glowed like a thick fog.
That old light is still all around us today.
A small part of the noise on an old television is this light.
After that, there were no stars, only dark clouds of gas.
Gravity slowly pulled the gas together into bigger and bigger balls.
Then the very first stars began to shine in the dark.
Inside a star, small atoms join together and give out energy.
Gravity pulls a star inward and its heat pushes outward.
Big stars burn fast and die young, but small stars live long.
Stars make new kinds of atoms, like carbon and oxygen.
At last, a giant star explodes in a huge flash.
Rare things like gold come from violent events in space.
The carbon in your body was made inside an old star.
Gravity pulled the stars together into great groups called galaxies.
Some galaxies are round, some are flat spirals, and some are messy.
We live in a galaxy called the Milky Way.
The Sun goes around the galaxy about once every two hundred million years.
On a dark night you can see the Milky Way as a pale band.
A black hole pulls so strongly that even light cannot escape.
One day, the Andromeda galaxy may crash into our own.
Galaxies spin as if they have much more stuff than we see.
Space is stretching faster and faster, and we do not know why.
Most of the Universe is made of things we cannot see.
Our Sun and planets began as a cloud of gas.
The cloud spun faster and flattened into a disc.
Dust stuck together and slowly grew into rocks, then into planets.
Planets near the Sun are small and rocky, and far ones are huge.
The Sun is a star, and it is much bigger than Earth.
Venus is the hottest planet, because its air traps the heat.
Mars is red, because its dust is like rust.
Jupiter is the biggest planet, and it is made of gas.
Saturn has beautiful rings made of ice and rock.
Far from the Sun there are icy worlds and comets.
The young Earth was so hot that rocks melted.
Heavy metal sank to the middle, and light rock stayed on top.
A small planet probably hit the young Earth long ago.
Astronauts brought back Moon rocks, and they are much like Earth rocks.
The Moon always shows the same face to the Earth.
The Moon pulls on the sea and makes the tides.
The Moon is moving away from us very slowly.
The Moon helps to keep the Earth's tilt steady.
Scientists use old rocks to find the age of the Earth.
The oldest bit of the Earth is a tiny crystal.
The Earth has layers, with a hot metal ball in the middle.
Earthquake waves travel through the Earth and show what is inside.
The middle of the Earth is as hot as the Sun's surface.
Hot rock under the ground moves, but extremely slowly.
The Earth's surface is made of big pieces called plates.
Plates can pull apart, push together, or slide past each other.
An earthquake happens when rock suddenly slips along a crack.
Hot melted rock rises and bursts out of a volcano.
When plates push together, mountains slowly rise up.
Long ago, all the land was joined in one huge continent.
Most of the air is nitrogen, and about one fifth is oxygen.
Most of the air lies close to the ground.
Oceans cover most of our planet, and the water is very old.
Ice floats on water, so fish can live under frozen lakes.
The Sun lifts water from the sea, and rain brings it back.
The Sun heats the Earth unevenly, and this makes wind.
Some gases in the air hold heat, like a blanket.
Burning coal, oil and gas puts carbon dioxide into the air.
Our world has become warmer by more than one degree.
Old ice holds bubbles of air from long, long ago.
Layers of rock and fossils tell us about the past.
If Earth's history were one year, people come at the very end.
Living things grow, use energy, and make new life.
Scientists once made parts of life from simple gases.
Nobody knows exactly where or how life began on Earth.
The oldest signs of life are very, very old.
The first living things were tiny cells with a thin skin.
Your body is made of trillions of tiny cells.
DNA is a code that holds the plans for a living thing.
Genes pass from parents to their children in a family.
Charles Darwin sailed around the world on a ship.
Living things differ, and the best suited ones leave more young.
Island birds have bills of many shapes to suit their food.
Some germs survive medicine, and then they make more germs.
Long ago, people turned wild wolves into pet dogs.
A monk grew peas and learned how features pass on.
Evolution has no plan, and it has no goal.
Fossils show how animals changed over a very long time.
DNA shows that all living things are related.
In science, a theory is an idea that has been tested a lot.
Tiny green living things used sunlight and made oxygen.
Over two billion years ago, oxygen began to fill the air.
One cell may have swallowed another, and the two lived together.
For a very long time, life was tiny and had one cell.
The first large animals were soft and lived in the sea.
About five hundred million years ago, new animals appeared quickly.
Some of these new animals had eyes, and some hunted others.
The first fish had a backbone, and they swam in the sea.
Plants moved from the water onto the land.
Later, animals crawled out of the water to live on land.
Long ago, great forests grew and huge insects flew.
Then a huge disaster killed most living things on Earth.
There have been five great extinctions in the history of life.
Dinosaurs first appeared about two hundred and thirty million years ago.
Some dinosaurs were huge, and some were as small as chickens.
Birds are the living family of the dinosaurs.
Tyrannosaurus rex was a huge hunter with very strong jaws.
Some famous reptiles of that time were not dinosaurs.
Then a huge rock from space hit the Earth.
Only the birds survived from the family of dinosaurs.
Small furry animals lived quietly next to the big dinosaurs.
Whales came from animals that once walked on land.
Some small mammals lived in trees and grew clever hands.
People and apes share the same very old family.
Lucy lived long ago, and she walked on two legs.
Early people made stone tools and learned to use fire.
Early humans walked out of Africa and spread across Asia.
The Neanderthals were close relatives of our own species.
Our species first appeared in Africa about three hundred thousand years ago.
Farming started eleven thousand years ago, and cities came later.
Tiny living things are everywhere, even on your skin.
Most of these tiny living things do not hurt you.
Long ago, people did not know that germs make us ill.
Washing your hands can stop the spread of germs.
In 1796, a doctor made the first vaccine, to fight smallpox.
A vaccine teaches the body how to fight a germ.
A mould in a dish killed the germs near it.
A virus is much smaller than a living cell.
Clean drinking water has saved millions of people from illness.
People today live much longer than people did long ago.
Long ago, some Greeks said everything is made of tiny bits.
Atoms are so small that you can never see them.
Every atom has a tiny centre, with smaller bits around it.
Almost all of an atom is empty space.
Each kind of atom is called an element.
The periodic table is a chart of all the elements.
Atoms join together to make bigger things called molecules.
In a chemical change, no atoms are lost or made.
Some atoms are not stable, and they slowly break apart.
The atoms in you were once part of other things.
Energy is what makes things move and change.
Energy is never lost, but it often changes into another kind.
Hot things have atoms that move very fast.
Heat always moves from hot things to cold things.
Your body gets energy from the food that you eat.
A moving thing keeps moving unless a force stops it.
A heavy thing is harder to push than a light one.
Every push has an equal push back the other way.
Friction slows things down when they rub together.
A tiny bit of matter can turn into a huge amount of energy.
A wave carries energy from one place to another.
White light is really made of many colours.
Light is only one small part of a very large family of waves.
A rubbed balloon can pick up small pieces of paper.
Electric current is a flow of tiny particles through a wire.
A compass points north because the Earth is a big magnet.
A moving magnet can push electricity along a wire.
Light is a wave made of electricity and magnets.
Light acts like a wave and also like tiny bits.
Most things in a big city need electricity to work.
The same force pulls an apple down and holds the Moon.
Astronauts float because they are always falling around the Earth.
A small magnet can lift a pin against the whole Earth.
Einstein said that heavy things bend space and time.
In 1919, scientists saw light from stars bend near the Sun.
Time passes a little faster in space than on the ground.
Nothing in the Universe can go faster than light.
In 2015, scientists detected ripples in space from two black holes.
Very tiny things do not behave like big things at all.
Quantum ideas gave us phones, computers and lasers.
Your brain is small, but it does an enormous amount of work.
Nerve cells pass tiny signals to each other.
Each nerve cell links to thousands of other cells.
Your brain builds the picture of the world that you see.
Different parts of the brain do different jobs.
Memories are not stored like photographs, and they can change.
You remember better when you review a little, often.
Your brain is still working hard when you are asleep.
Reading is new, and your brain learned to do it.
Nobody knows exactly how a brain makes a mind.
Science starts when someone asks a good question.
A Greek man measured the whole Earth with a stick.
A fair test changes only one thing at a time.
Sometimes scientists find that a famous idea is wrong.
Scientists must be ready to say that they were wrong.
Once, some scientists thought that something went faster than light.
Science cannot answer every question, and that is fine.
Many big questions are still waiting for answers.
Your body is made of atoms that came from the stars.
You are part of this story, so keep asking questions.
B1B2: Every school has to leave things out, because there is far more to know than any timetable can hold. This book is a quick tour of the big ideas that you may have missed.
Far from city lights, a clear night shows a few thousand stars to the naked eye. Every one of them belongs to our own galaxy, and each one is a sun, very far away.

Light is the fastest thing we know, and it travels about three hundred thousand kilometres every second. The Moon is nearly four hundred thousand kilometres away, so its light reaches you in a little over a second.
The Sun is about one hundred and fifty million kilometres away. Its light needs a little over eight minutes to cross that gap, so you always see the Sun as it was eight minutes ago.
Kilometres are too small for measuring space, so scientists use the light year instead. It is the distance that light travels in one year, which is about nine and a half trillion kilometres.
The nearest star after the Sun is Proxima Centauri, a little more than four light years away. The spacecraft that we have sent into deep space would need tens of thousands of years to get there.
Light takes time to travel, so distant things look as they were long ago. The Andromeda galaxy, which you can just see in a dark sky, appears as it was about two and a half million years ago.
The part of the Universe that we can see is about ninety billion light years across. Beyond it there may be much more, but its light has not had time to reach us.

The Hubble Space Telescope once stared at one tiny, empty-looking patch of sky for days and found thousands of galaxies. Astronomers think the observable Universe holds hundreds of billions of them, each with billions of stars.
In this book we will start with the whole Universe and then come down to Earth. After that we will explore life, atoms and energy, and then finish with the brain that is reading this.

About a hundred years ago, Edwin Hubble showed that other galaxies lie far outside our own. Soon afterwards the light from them showed that almost all are moving away from us, and the farther they are, the faster they go.

If the galaxies are moving apart now, then in the past they were closer together. Run the film all the way backwards and everything was once squeezed into a space that was incredibly small, hot and dense.

Scientists calculate that the Universe began nearly fourteen billion years ago, from a state that was extremely hot and dense. We call that beginning the Big Bang, and it was the start of space and time as we know them.
The Big Bang was not an explosion in the middle of empty space. Think of raisins in rising dough: as it swells, every raisin moves away from all the others, and none is the centre.
Scientists can describe the early Universe very well, but they cannot yet say what came before it. Time itself may have started then, in which case the question may not even make sense.
In the first tiny fraction of a second, the Universe was hotter than the centre of any star. Many scientists think it also grew by an enormous amount in that instant, in a burst called inflation.
As the Universe cooled, protons and neutrons began to stick together. Within about three minutes it had made the centres of hydrogen and helium atoms, mostly hydrogen, with about a quarter helium.

For about three hundred and eighty thousand years the Universe was like a glowing fog, because free electrons kept scattering light. Then it cooled enough for atoms to form, and light was suddenly free to travel across space.

That first light has been cooling for nearly fourteen billion years, and today it is a faint glow of microwaves coming from every direction. Two radio engineers found it by accident in 1965, while trying to remove a hiss from their antenna.

If you tuned an old analogue television between channels, about one per cent of the speckled static you saw came from the Big Bang. Together with the moving galaxies and the mix of atoms, this afterglow is why most scientists trust the theory.
When the first glow faded, the Universe went dark, with no stars yet to light it. Clouds of hydrogen and helium drifted through the gloom for many millions of years.
Gravity is the pull that every piece of matter has on every other. In the thicker patches of gas it pulled harder, so over millions of years the clouds shrank and grew denser.
Perhaps a hundred or two hundred million years after the Big Bang, the first stars switched on. They were probably very large and very hot, and they shone with a bright blue-white light.
When gas is squeezed hard enough, it becomes hot enough for atoms to crash together. In a star this is called fusion: hydrogen atoms join to make helium and release huge amounts of energy.
A star is held in a long balance between two forces. Gravity pulls its gas inward, while the heat from fusion pushes it outward, and for millions or billions of years the two forces match.
The heaviest stars use up their fuel in only a few million years. Small red stars burn slowly and could shine for trillions of years, much longer than the Universe has existed.

As a star ages, it fuses helium into carbon and oxygen, and the biggest stars go on to make heavier atoms still. The inside of a large old star is layered like an onion, with the heaviest atoms at the centre.
Fusing iron does not release energy, so it is where a giant star's fuel finally runs out. The core collapses in a fraction of a second, and the star blows apart in an explosion called a supernova.
Supernovae scatter the carbon, oxygen and iron from a star into space. Heavier metals such as gold come from even more violent events, and in 2017 astronomers saw two neutron stars collide.
The hydrogen in your body dates from the Big Bang. Almost everything else, from the calcium in your bones to the iron in your blood, was made in stars that died before the Sun existed.
Gravity did not stop with single stars, but went on to gather them. It pulled stars, gas and dust into huge families called galaxies, and young galaxies often merged to become larger ones.

Galaxies come in three main shapes, and astronomers have a name for each one. Spirals have curling arms like a whirlpool, ellipticals are smooth ovals, and irregular galaxies have no clear shape at all.
Our galaxy is the Milky Way, a spiral that holds a few hundred billion stars. It is about a hundred thousand light years across, and the Sun lies in one of its arms, far from the centre.
The Sun and its planets move around the centre of the galaxy at more than two hundred kilometres every second. Even at that speed, one trip takes roughly two hundred and thirty million years.
The pale band across a dark sky is the Milky Way. You are looking along the flat disc of your galaxy from inside, so billions of stars blur into a cloud of light.
A black hole is a place where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape. At the centre of the Milky Way sits one that is about four million times as heavy as the Sun.
The Andromeda galaxy is moving toward the Milky Way. Astronomers think the two may merge in several billion years, although the stars are so far apart that few if any would actually collide.
The stars at the edge of a galaxy move much too fast for the gravity of what we can see. Scientists conclude that galaxies hold a great deal of unseen matter, which they call dark matter.
In the late 1990s, astronomers watching distant exploding stars found that the expansion of the Universe is speeding up. They named the unknown cause dark energy, and it is still a deep mystery.

Atoms like those in you and the stars make up only about five per cent of the Universe. About a quarter is dark matter and almost seventy per cent is dark energy, and nobody yet knows what either one is.
About four and a half billion years ago, a huge cloud of gas and dust began to collapse. Something, perhaps a nearby exploding star, may have nudged it, and its centre grew hot and dense.
As the cloud shrank, it spun faster, like a skater pulling in her arms. It flattened into a disc, and almost all of its matter fell into the middle to form the Sun.
In the disc, tiny grains of dust stuck together and grew into pebbles, then boulders, then mountain-sized lumps. Their gravity pulled in more, and after millions of years they had become planets.

Near the hot young Sun, only rock and metal could stay solid, so the inner planets are small and rocky. Farther out, ice could form too, and the giant planets grew large enough to hold thick coats of gas.
The Sun is about one hundred and nine times wider than the Earth, and more than a million Earths could fit inside it. Even so, it is only an average star, and it is about halfway through its life.

Mercury is the smallest planet and has hardly any air, so its days are scorching and its nights freezing. Venus is even hotter, because its thick carbon dioxide air holds the surface at about four hundred and sixty degrees Celsius.
Mars looks red because its soil contains iron that has rusted. Long ago it had rivers and lakes, but today its water is mostly frozen and its air is thin.
Jupiter is more than twice as heavy as all the other planets put together. Its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than the Earth, and it has been seen swirling for centuries.

Saturn's famous rings are made of billions of pieces of ice, from tiny grains to lumps as big as houses. Far beyond it, Uranus and Neptune are cold blue giants, and Neptune has the fastest winds in the Solar System.
Beyond Neptune lies a cold zone full of icy bodies, home to the dwarf planet Pluto. Comets, which are lumps of ice and dust, come from there and perhaps from a cloud that nobody has yet seen.
The young Earth was built from countless crashes, and each crash gave off heat. For a long time its surface was a sea of glowing melted rock, with no ocean and no solid ground.
While the Earth was still molten, heavy iron and nickel sank to the centre. Lighter rock floated above it, and in this way the planet sorted itself into layers.
The best idea so far is that a planet about the size of Mars crashed into the young Earth. Scientists call it Theia, and the cloud of melted rock thrown into space gathered into the Moon.

Between 1969 and 1972, American astronauts brought home about three hundred and eighty kilograms of Moon rock. It is chemically very like the rock in Earth's outer layers, which supports the idea of a giant crash.
The Moon turns once on its axis in exactly the time it takes to go once around the Earth. That is why we always see the same face, and the far side can be seen only from space.
The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans and makes the water bulge. As the Earth turns, most coasts have two high tides and two low tides each day.

Astronauts left mirrors on the Moon, and scientists bounce laser beams off them. They have found that the Moon moves away from the Earth by about four centimetres every year, roughly as fast as a fingernail grows.

The Earth leans over by about twenty-three degrees, and that lean gives us the seasons. Many scientists think the Moon's gravity keeps the lean steady, which has probably helped to keep our climate stable.

Some atoms in rocks change slowly into other atoms at a steady rate, which is called radioactive decay. By measuring that change, scientists have found that the Earth is about four and a half billion years old.

The oldest known pieces of the young Earth are tiny crystals called zircons, found in Western Australia. They are nearly four and a half billion years old, and they hint that the planet already had a solid crust and liquid water.

The Earth has four layers: a thin crust, a thick mantle of hot rock, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core. The deepest hole ever drilled is about twelve kilometres deep, while the centre is more than six thousand kilometres down.
When an earthquake strikes, waves of shaking travel right through the planet. Instruments around the world record them, and the way the waves bend and stop has shown scientists what lies deep below.
The inner core is a ball of iron and nickel, a little smaller than the Moon. It is as hot as the surface of the Sun, but it stays solid because the pressure on it is crushing.
The mantle is solid rock, but over millions of years it flows like very thick syrup. Hot rock rises, cooler rock sinks, and this slow stirring moves the crust above.

The Earth's crust is broken into several huge plates and many smaller ones, like the pieces of a cracked eggshell. They carry the continents and oceans, and they move only a few centimetres each year.
Plates can pull apart, push together or slide past each other, and each kind of meeting builds something different. Most of the world's earthquakes and volcanoes happen along these edges.
Plates do not slide smoothly, because their edges catch on each other. Pressure builds up for years, and then the rock suddenly slips and shakes the ground in an earthquake.
A volcano forms where melted rock called magma finds a way to the surface. Many of the world's volcanoes lie in a great ring around the Pacific Ocean, known as the Ring of Fire.
About fifty million years ago, India crashed slowly into Asia, and the crust crumpled upward to form the Himalayas. They are still rising by a few millimetres each year.

About three hundred million years ago, nearly all the land was joined as one supercontinent called Pangaea. In 1912 Alfred Wegener said that the continents drift, but he was ignored until sea-floor evidence arrived in the 1960s.
The air around you is about seventy-eight per cent nitrogen and twenty-one per cent oxygen. The last one per cent is mostly argon, with tiny amounts of carbon dioxide and water vapour.
The atmosphere is much thinner than most people imagine. Half of all the air lies below about five and a half kilometres, so near the top of Mount Everest breathing is hard.
Oceans cover about seventy per cent of the Earth's surface. Where all that water came from is debated, with comets, asteroids and the young Earth's own rocks all suggested as sources.
Most solids sink in their own liquid, but ice floats on water because it is lighter. Lakes freeze from the top down, and the water underneath stays liquid so that fish survive the winter.
The Sun warms the sea and lifts water into the air as vapour. It cools into clouds and falls again as rain, and the water you drink is billions of years old.
The Sun heats the equator more than the poles, and it heats land and sea differently. Warm air rises and cool air rushes in to replace it, and that movement is what we call wind.
Gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour let sunlight in but slow the escape of heat. This greenhouse effect is helpful, because without it the Earth would be about thirty degrees colder.

Carbon moves in a great cycle through air, plants, animals, oceans and rocks. Coal, oil and gas are the remains of ancient life, and when we burn them we quickly put their stored carbon back into the air.

Before factories and engines, the air held about two hundred and eighty parts per million of carbon dioxide. Today it holds more than four hundred and twenty, and the Earth has warmed by a little over one degree Celsius.

Deep in Antarctica, scientists drill ice cores that hold bubbles of air from up to eight hundred thousand years ago. They show that ice ages came and went with the carbon dioxide, and that today's level is higher than at any time in that record.
Rock forms in layers, and the lower layers are usually older than the ones above them. Fossils, the remains or traces of ancient life, are found in those layers and show what lived when.
Imagine Earth's history squeezed into one year, with the planet forming on the first of January. Life appears by March, and modern people arrive only in the last forty minutes of the final day.

Scientists find life surprisingly hard to define in a few words. Most agree that living things use energy, grow, respond to their surroundings and make copies of themselves, and that their descendants slowly change.

In 1953, a young chemist sent electric sparks through a flask of water and simple gases, imitating the early Earth. Within days it contained amino acids, which are the building blocks of the proteins in living things.
Some scientists think that life began in warm shallow pools, and others point to hot vents on the sea floor. A few suggest it started on the surfaces of clay, but none of these ideas has been proved.

Among the oldest signs of life are layered mounds built by microbes in Western Australian rocks about three and a half billion years old. Some chemical traces may be older, but experts still argue about them.
A cell is a bag of chemicals wrapped in a thin skin, and it is the smallest unit of life. The first cells were simple, and for billions of years every living thing was a single cell.
In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at cork through a microscope and called the little boxes he saw cells. Scientists now estimate that a human body contains about thirty-seven trillion of them.

DNA is a long molecule shaped like a twisted ladder, and it carries the instructions for building a living thing. Its shape was worked out in 1953, with the help of X-ray pictures taken by Rosalind Franklin.

A gene is a stretch of DNA with the recipe for one protein, and proteins do most of the work in a cell. You received half of your genes from each parent, along with a few tiny changes that nobody else has.

In 1831, a young Englishman named Charles Darwin set sail on the ship Beagle. During almost five years of travel he collected plants, animals and fossils, and he saw how living things differ from place to place.

Darwin's idea of natural selection has three simple steps. Living things vary, those whose features suit their surroundings survive and breed more often, and they pass those features on to their young.
On the Galapagos Islands, finches have beaks of many shapes, each suited to a different food. Scientists who measured them for decades saw the average beak change within a few years after a drought.

When a drug kills most of the bacteria in a patient, any that happen to resist it survive and multiply. Over time whole populations become resistant, which is natural selection happening in a hospital.

Dogs are descended from wolves, and people have shaped them for many thousands of years by choosing which animals would breed. Chihuahuas and Great Danes are both the result of this selection, and they belong to the same species.
In the 1860s, a monk named Gregor Mendel grew thousands of pea plants and counted the results. He found that features are passed on in separate units, which we now call genes.

Mutations happen by chance, but natural selection is not random, because it keeps what works. Evolution has no goal and no plan, and it makes living things better suited to where they live, not better in every way.
Fossils show how groups of animals changed over time. One example is Tiktaalik, a fish about three hundred and seventy-five million years old, with strong fins that could prop up its body like limbs.

Comparing the DNA of different species is like comparing family records. Humans share about ninety-eight per cent of their DNA with chimpanzees, many genes with mice, and even some with bananas and yeast.

In everyday talk a theory is only a guess, but in science it means an explanation that has been tested many times. Evolution, like gravity, is a theory in that strong sense, and it is supported by fossils, DNA and direct observation.

Cyanobacteria are tiny living things that use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make food, in a process called photosynthesis. They give off oxygen as waste, and they began doing this billions of years ago.
At first the oxygen reacted with iron in the sea and turned it to rust, which sank to the bottom. Then, about two and a half billion years ago, the oxygen began to build up in the air.

Complex cells have a nucleus and tiny power stations called mitochondria. Many scientists think that mitochondria were once free bacteria that were taken inside another cell, perhaps about two billion years ago.
For about three billion years, nearly all life stayed microscopic. Then, in several different groups, cells began sticking together and sharing the work, and so many-celled life began.

Between about five hundred and seventy and five hundred and forty million years ago, strange soft creatures lay on the sea floor. Some looked like leaves or quilts, and scientists are still unsure how they relate to later animals.

About five hundred and forty million years ago, the fossil record suddenly fills with animals that have shells, legs and spines. Within about twenty million years, most of the main animal groups had appeared, in what is called the Cambrian explosion.

The Cambrian sea held hunters, armoured trilobites and some of the first animals with complex eyes. We know about them in great detail because the Burgess Shale in Canada preserved even their soft parts.

Among the early animals were small fish-like creatures, and by about five hundred million years ago some had a backbone. Later fish developed jaws, which helped them to become the most successful hunters in the sea.
About four hundred and seventy million years ago, small plants like mosses began to live on land. Together with fungi, they helped to break up bare rock and build the first real soil.

Small animals such as early insects and spiders reached the land about four hundred and thirty million years ago. Some fish with strong fins later became four-legged animals and followed them about three hundred and seventy million years ago.

About three hundred million years ago, steamy swamp forests covered much of the land. Their dead trees were buried and slowly turned into coal, and some dragonfly-like insects had wings as wide as a pigeon's.

About two hundred and fifty-two million years ago came the worst extinction of all, known as the Great Dying. Probably because of enormous volcanic eruptions in Siberia, most species on Earth disappeared.
Scientists recognise five great mass extinctions, each of which wiped out a large share of the world's species. After each one, the survivors spread into empty places, and new kinds of life appeared.
After the Great Dying, reptiles of many kinds filled the land. The first dinosaurs appeared about two hundred and thirty million years ago, and they were small, fast animals that walked on two legs.
The biggest long-necked dinosaurs weighed more than ten elephants, while some others were the size of a chicken. Fossils found in China show that many of the smaller ones were covered in feathers.

About a hundred and fifty million years ago, Archaeopteryx, a creature the size of a magpie, had feathered wings, teeth and a long bony tail. Scientists now agree that birds descend from small feathered dinosaurs, so every bird is a living dinosaur.
Tyrannosaurus rex was about twelve metres long, with jaws strong enough to crush bone. It lived about sixty-six million years ago, which is closer to us in time than to Stegosaurus.

Reptiles also lived in the sea and in the air, but those great swimmers and flyers were not dinosaurs. Plesiosaurs hunted in the water, and pterosaurs, the first backboned animals to fly, soared overhead.
About sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid about ten kilometres wide hit what is now Mexico. It left a crater about a hundred and eighty kilometres across, and its impact changed the whole world.

In 1980, scientists found a thin layer of clay rich in iridium, in rocks from that very time. Iridium is rare on the Earth's surface but common in asteroids, and the same layer was found around the world.

Mammals had lived alongside the dinosaurs for more than a hundred million years, mostly as small animals that hid or hunted at night. After the asteroid, many of them survived, and the empty world gave them room to grow.

About fifty million years ago, the ancestors of whales were four-legged animals that walked on land and waded into water. Fossils from India and Pakistan show their legs growing smaller over millions of years.

Early primates, the group that includes monkeys, apes and humans, appeared more than fifty million years ago. They lived in trees, with grasping hands, forward-facing eyes and large brains for their size.

Humans are apes, and our closest living relatives are the chimpanzees and bonobos. We did not come from them: both groups descend from a shared ancestor that lived about six to seven million years ago.
In 1974, scientists in Ethiopia found the bones of Lucy, who lived about three million years ago. She was only about one metre tall, but her leg and hip bones show that she walked upright.

Early members of our own genus, Homo, were making stone tools about two and a half million years ago. They also learned to use fire, at least a million years ago, which gave them warmth, protection and cooked food.

Homo erectus, who stood tall and walked far, appeared nearly two million years ago. They were the first humans to leave Africa, and their fossils have been found in places as far apart as Georgia and Indonesia.

Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia for hundreds of thousands of years, and they made tools, used fire and cared for each other. Most people outside Africa carry about two per cent Neanderthal DNA, because their ancestors had children with them.
Our own species, Homo sapiens, appeared in Africa about three hundred thousand years ago. Over a very long time, some groups moved out into Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas.

Farming began about eleven thousand years ago, and the first cities and writing appeared roughly five thousand years ago. That is less than a blink in the story of the Earth, yet almost everything we call history happened then.
Microbes are living things too small to see, and they are everywhere: in soil, in water, in the air and on your skin. A human body carries about as many bacterial cells as human ones.
Only a small share of microbes make people ill. Many live in your gut and help to digest food, and others make vitamins or train the body's defences.
For centuries people blamed bad air and bad luck for disease. In the 1800s, scientists such as Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch showed that particular germs cause particular illnesses.

In 1847 a doctor in Vienna, Ignaz Semmelweis, noticed that mothers died less often when doctors washed their hands first. Many of his colleagues refused to believe him, because germs were not yet understood.

In 1796, an English doctor, Edward Jenner, showed that a mild disease called cowpox could protect people from the deadly smallpox. Using vaccines, the world beat smallpox, and in 1980 it was declared gone.
Your immune system is a team of cells that attacks germs. A vaccine shows it a harmless piece or copy of a germ in advance, so that it can respond quickly if the real one arrives.
In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould had killed the bacteria around it in a dish. Other scientists later turned that mould's chemical, penicillin, into the first widely used antibiotic.
A virus is a tiny package of genes inside a protein coat, and it is much smaller than a bacterium. It cannot copy itself, so it enters a cell and uses the cell's machinery to make more viruses.

In 1854 a London doctor, John Snow, mapped the homes of people with cholera and found that they clustered round one water pump. When the pump was shut, the outbreak faded, and later cities built sewers and clean water supplies.

In 1800, the average person in the world could expect to live only about thirty to thirty-five years, mostly because so many children died young. Today the figure is over seventy, thanks to better food, clean water, vaccines and medicines.
Nearly twenty-five centuries ago, the Greek thinker Democritus said that cutting something again and again must end at a piece that cannot be cut. He called it an atom, a word meaning uncuttable.
Atoms are far too small to see, even with a normal microscope. A single hair is about half a million atoms wide, and the dot over the letter i holds trillions of them.
Every atom has a tiny nucleus in the middle, made of protons and neutrons. Much lighter electrons move around it, and protons have a positive charge while electrons have a negative one.

If an atom were as big as a football stadium, its nucleus would be a grain of sand in the middle. In 1911 Ernest Rutherford found this by firing tiny particles at gold foil, and most went straight through.
An element is one kind of atom, and what makes it different is the number of protons in its nucleus. Hydrogen has one proton, carbon has six, and gold has seventy-nine.

In 1869 the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the known elements in a table, so that similar ones fell in the same column. He left gaps for elements nobody had found, and he was proved right when they were discovered.

Atoms join together by sharing or swapping tiny particles called electrons. When two hydrogen atoms bond with one oxygen atom, they make a molecule of water, which behaves nothing like either gas on its own.
When a candle burns, it seems to disappear into thin air. In truth its atoms combine with oxygen and become carbon dioxide and water vapour, and not a single atom is lost.

Some atoms have unstable nuclei, and they slowly give out energy as radiation while changing into other atoms. Marie Curie studied this radioactivity around 1900, and today it is used for dating rocks and for medical scans.
Atoms are never used up, only moved from place to place. The carbon in your body has been in the air and in plants, and perhaps in other animals, before it came to you.
Energy is the ability to make something change or move. It comes in many forms, including movement, heat, light, sound and the energy stored in food, fuel and batteries.
When you throw a ball, the energy in your muscles becomes the ball's movement, and then a little heat as it lands. The total never changes, and this rule is called the conservation of energy.
Heat is the energy of tiny atoms jiggling about, and temperature tells us how fast they move. The coldest possible temperature is about minus two hundred and seventy-three degrees Celsius.
Heat flows from hot things to cold things, and never the other way by itself. Scientists describe this with the idea of entropy, which says that nature tends to move from order toward disorder.
The food you eat holds chemical energy, which was first captured from sunlight by plants. Your cells use oxygen to release that energy slowly, and some of it keeps your body warm.
In 1687 Isaac Newton published the laws that describe how things move. His first law says that an object keeps moving in a straight line at a steady speed, unless a force acts on it.
Newton's second law says that the harder you push something, the faster it speeds up. A heavier object needs a bigger push to change its motion by the same amount.

Newton's third law says that when one object pushes on another, the second pushes back equally hard in the opposite direction. A rocket flies by pushing hot gas downward, and the gas pushes the rocket upward.
Friction is the force that resists when two surfaces rub together. It slows a sliding box, but without it you could not walk, because your feet would slip like skates on ice.

In 1905 Albert Einstein showed that mass is a very concentrated form of energy, and his famous equation says how much. The Sun turns about four million tonnes of its matter into light and heat every second.
A wave carries energy from place to place, without carrying the water or air along with it. Sound is a wave in the air, and it travels at about three hundred and forty metres every second.

In the 1660s Isaac Newton passed sunlight through a glass prism and showed that white light is a mixture of all the colours. A rainbow forms in the same way, when raindrops split sunlight into its colours.
Visible light is just a narrow slice of a much larger family of waves. Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all the same kind of wave, but with different lengths.
Electrons carry a negative charge and protons a positive one, and opposite charges attract. When you rub a balloon on your hair, electrons move across, and the balloon can then stick to a wall.
An electric current is a flow of electrons through a wire. A battery pushes them round a complete circle, and they give up energy as they pass through a bulb, a motor or a heater.
Every magnet has two poles, and unlike poles attract each other. The Earth acts like a giant magnet, powered by the liquid iron in its core, and that is why a compass needle points north.
In 1831 Michael Faraday found that moving a magnet near a coil of wire makes an electric current flow. Most of the electricity that we use is made in this way, by machines called generators.

In the 1860s the Scottish scientist James Clerk Maxwell wrote equations that joined electricity and magnetism into one theory. They predicted waves that travel at the speed of light, and he realised that light itself must be such a wave.
