In 1905 Einstein showed that light also comes in tiny packets of energy, now called photons. When photons hit a metal plate they can knock electrons loose, and that is how a solar panel makes electricity.
Electricity lights our homes, runs our phones and trains, and carries our messages across the world. About nine in every ten people alive today have access to it.
A famous story says that Isaac Newton saw an apple fall and began to think. He realised that the force pulling the apple to the ground, gravity, also keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth.

At the height of a space station, gravity is still almost as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because they and the station are falling together, while moving sideways so fast that they keep missing the Earth.
Gravity is the weakest of the four basic forces of nature. A small fridge magnet can lift a paperclip against the pull of the entire Earth, but gravity wins at large scales.
In 1915 Albert Einstein proposed a new idea of gravity. Mass bends space and time, he said, and things follow the curves, just as a marble rolls around a dent in a stretched sheet.
Einstein's idea made a bold prediction: starlight passing close to the Sun should bend. In 1919, during a total eclipse, astronomers measured the shift and found that he was right.

Einstein's theory says that time runs slightly slower where gravity is stronger, and experiments have confirmed it. Satellites for GPS must correct for this, or the maps on our phones would drift by kilometres every day.

Nothing can travel faster than light, and the nearer an object gets to that speed, the more its clock slows down. This has been shown with fast particles and with clocks carried around the Earth in aeroplanes.

Einstein predicted that moving masses make ripples in space, called gravitational waves. In 2015, almost a century later, huge instruments felt the ripples from two black holes that had merged more than a billion years earlier.
At the scale of atoms, nature follows strange rules called quantum physics. Energy comes in tiny packets, and we cannot know both the exact position and the exact speed of a particle at once.

Quantum physics explains how transistors and lasers work, so it lies behind every phone and computer. Yet it does not fit together with Einstein's picture of gravity, and joining the two is one of the great unsolved problems of science.
An adult brain weighs about one and a half kilograms, roughly the same as a large bottle of water. It holds about eighty-six billion nerve cells, and it uses about a fifth of the body's energy.

A nerve cell, or neuron, has branches that collect signals and a long fibre that sends them on. Inside a neuron the signal is a tiny electrical pulse, and between neurons it is carried by chemical messengers.
Each neuron can connect to thousands of others, so the brain has at least a hundred trillion connections. What you know is stored in the pattern of those connections, not in the cells alone.

The lens of the eye makes an upside-down image on the back of the eye. Your brain turns the signals into the picture you see, and even colour is something that the brain creates from light of different lengths.

The wrinkled outer layer of the brain, the cortex, handles thinking, language and the senses. The cerebellum at the back helps with balance and movement, and the brainstem controls breathing and the heartbeat.

A part of the brain called the hippocampus helps to form new memories, which are then stored across many regions. Each time you remember something, your brain partly rebuilds it, which is why memories can change over the years.

When you learn something, connections between neurons grow stronger, and practice strengthens them further. In the 1880s Hermann Ebbinghaus found that we forget quickly at first, but that reviewing after gaps helps memories to last.
During sleep the brain is far from switched off. It replays and sorts the day's learning, and most adults function best on about seven to nine hours of sleep each night.
Children learn to speak just by listening to the people around them. Writing is only about five thousand years old, so the brain did not evolve for reading, but it can learn to read with practice.

Scientists can link many mental activities to particular patterns in the brain. How all that electrical activity becomes the feeling of being you, which is called consciousness, is still one of the biggest open questions.
Science begins with curiosity: someone notices something odd and asks why. The best questions are the ones that can be tested, so that evidence can decide the answer.

About two thousand two hundred years ago, the Greek scholar Eratosthenes compared the shadows of sticks in two Egyptian cities. From the difference and the distance between them, he calculated the size of the whole Earth.

To test an idea, scientists make a hypothesis, which is a guess that can be checked. Then they run a fair experiment that changes only one thing at a time, so that they know what caused any difference.

For decades most doctors believed that stress and spicy food caused stomach ulcers. In the 1980s two Australian doctors showed that a bacterium was the real cause of many ulcers, and they won a Nobel Prize in 2005.
A good scientist tries hard to prove her own ideas wrong. When the evidence disagrees with a favourite idea, the idea has to go, and finding a mistake counts as progress.

In 2011 a team in Europe measured tiny particles that seemed to travel faster than light, and they asked the whole world to check their work. The mistake turned out to be a loose cable in the timing equipment.
Science is very good at explaining how the world works, but it cannot tell us what is right or what we should value. It also admits when we do not know, and that honesty is part of its strength.

Big questions remain open: what dark matter is, how life began, how a brain makes a mind, and how gravity fits with quantum physics. Perhaps the person who solves one of them is reading this book now.

Look at your hand and think about where it came from: its atoms were made in stars, and its cells descend from the first life. A brain that can understand that is one of the most remarkable results the Universe has produced.
Your atoms came from the stars, your cells came from ancient life, and your brain can now ask how it all works. You missed nothing for good, because the questions are still there for you.
C1C2: Think back to your school days, to the long afternoons and the clock above the board, and you may notice how much was quietly left out. No timetable can hold everything, so the great story of how the Universe, the Earth and life itself came to be usually arrived in scraps. This book gathers those scraps into one journey, beginning with the very largest question and working steadily down to the very small.

Away from the glow of the cities, a clear and moonless night reveals a few thousand stars scattered across the dark like spilled salt. All of them belong to our own galaxy, and every one is a sun, burning at a distance that makes the whole sky look quiet and still. The rest of the Universe is far too faint to see without help, which is why the sky looks so much emptier than it really is.

Nothing we know moves faster than light, which covers about three hundred thousand kilometres in a single second. The Moon lies nearly four hundred thousand kilometres from us, so the silver glow you see tonight left its surface a little more than a second ago. Even our nearest neighbour in space is therefore seen as it was, not quite as it is.

The Sun lies about one hundred and fifty million kilometres from Earth, a distance that feels enormous to us and is tiny by the standards of space. A beam of sunlight needs a little more than eight minutes to cross it. If the Sun were to vanish this instant, we would carry on enjoying its warmth and light for those same eight minutes.

Because the distances between the stars are so great, kilometres quickly become useless, and astronomers measure space with the light year instead. This is the distance that a beam of light covers in one year, roughly nine and a half trillion kilometres. A light year is therefore a measure of distance and not of time, even though the word year appears in its name.

The closest star beyond the Sun is a faint red one called Proxima Centauri, which lies a little more than four light years away. The spacecraft that we have already sent out into deep space travel so slowly by comparison that they would need tens of thousands of years to reach it. Space is not merely big; it is so empty that the gaps between the stars are most of what it contains.

Since light takes time to arrive, every telescope is also a kind of time machine, showing things as they once were rather than as they are. The Andromeda galaxy, a faint smudge that sharp eyes can find on a dark night, is shown to us as it looked about two and a half million years ago. Astronomers use this delay on purpose, because the farther they look, the further back into the story of the Universe they can see.

The part of the Universe that we can observe stretches about ninety billion light years from side to side, a figure that is larger than the age of the Universe suggests because space itself has been stretching. Beyond that edge there may be far more, possibly without end, but its light has had no time to reach us. We call the visible part the observable Universe, and it is only the region from which news can have arrived.

Once, astronomers aimed the Hubble Space Telescope for many days at one tiny patch of sky that looked completely empty, and the picture came back crowded with thousands of galaxies. From such samples they estimate that the observable Universe holds hundreds of billions of galaxies, each with millions or billions of stars. Nobody can count that many, so the true number remains an estimate that is argued over and revised from time to time.

Our journey starts with the whole Universe and its beginning, then narrows to a single star, a single planet and the thin film of life on its surface. From there it moves inward, to cells, to atoms and to the forces that hold everything together, and finally to the brain that is reading these words. At every step the facts are real, and wherever scientists are still unsure, you will be told so honestly.

In the 1920s the astronomer Edwin Hubble proved that the faint smudges in the sky were other galaxies, lying far beyond our own. Their light was stretched toward the red end of the spectrum, which showed that almost all of them are rushing away from us. What was more, the farther away a galaxy was, the faster it seemed to recede, which is exactly what a swelling Universe would produce.

Imagine playing the expansion of the Universe like a film and then running it backwards. The galaxies slide together, the gaps close, and the whole of space shrinks into something unimaginably small, hot and dense. That simple idea, followed to its conclusion, became the starting point for the Big Bang theory.

By measuring how fast the Universe is expanding today and working backwards, scientists calculate that everything began nearly fourteen billion years ago. We call that beginning the Big Bang, though the name makes it sound like a firework. In truth it was the start of space and time as we know them, rapidly stretching from an extremely hot and dense state.

It is tempting to picture the Big Bang as a bomb going off in a dark room, but that picture is wrong. Instead, imagine raisins in a loaf of rising dough: as the dough swells, every raisin drifts away from every other, and none of them is the centre. Space itself is what is stretching, so the Big Bang happened everywhere at once rather than at a single spot.

Physicists can describe the young Universe in remarkable detail, yet they cannot say what, if anything, came before it. Time itself may have begun at that moment, in which case asking what happened earlier is a little like asking what lies north of the North Pole. For now the honest answer is that nobody knows, and the question remains open for future scientists.

In its first tiny fraction of a second, the Universe was hotter than the heart of any star, and nothing like matter as we know it could yet exist. Many scientists think it also underwent a brief and violent burst of growth called inflation, stretching it by an enormous amount almost instantly. The evidence for inflation is promising but not settled, so it remains an idea that is still being tested.

As the young Universe cooled, protons and neutrons collided and began to stick together. Within the first few minutes, they had built the centres of hydrogen and helium atoms, and then the temperature dropped too far for any more building. The result was a Universe made of about three parts hydrogen to one part helium by weight, with only the faintest traces of anything heavier.

For its first three hundred and eighty thousand years, the Universe was a glowing, opaque fog, because loose electrons scattered every beam of light before it could go far. Then it cooled enough for electrons to settle into atoms, and the fog cleared almost at once. Light poured out in every direction, and some of it has been travelling ever since.

That ancient light has been stretched by the expanding Universe until it is now a faint glow of microwaves, arriving from every direction at once. Two radio engineers in America discovered it by accident in 1965, when they spent months trying to get rid of a stubborn hiss in their antenna. The hiss was the oldest light we can see, and it matched what the Big Bang theory had predicted.

On an old analogue television tuned between channels, perhaps one per cent of the speckled snow on the screen was this ancient light finally arriving. Together with the expansion of the galaxies and the ratio of hydrogen to helium, it forms the main support for the Big Bang theory. Three separate lines of evidence all point to the same story, and that is why almost every scientist who studies the subject accepts it.

Once the fog had cleared and its glow had cooled, the Universe slipped into a long darkness with no stars to light it. Vast clouds of hydrogen and helium drifted through the gloom, thinner in some places and slightly thicker in others. Those small differences in thickness would turn out to matter more than anything else.

Gravity is the pull that every piece of matter exerts on every other piece, and in the denser patches of gas it worked a little harder. Slowly, over millions of years, those patches drew in more and more of their surroundings and grew thicker still. A cloud that began as a loose, cold haze was turning into something heavy and hot.

Somewhere between a hundred and two hundred million years after the Big Bang, the first stars flickered into life. They were probably enormous, many times heavier than our Sun, and they burned fiercely with a blue-white light. No one has seen them directly, but powerful new telescopes are now beginning to catch glimpses of galaxies from that early dawn.

As a cloud of gas shrinks, the squeezing makes its centre hotter and hotter, until atoms are moving so fast that they smash together and stick. This process is called fusion, and in an ordinary star it turns hydrogen into helium while releasing an enormous amount of energy. That energy is the reason a star shines, and it is why the Sun can warm a planet from so far away.

Every star lives by a delicate balancing act between two great forces, and neither is ever allowed to win. Gravity pulls its gas inwards with relentless strength, while the heat from fusion at its core pushes outwards with equal force, and for millions or even billions of years neither side wins. A star dies when it can no longer keep that balance going, and how it ends depends on how heavy it was.

Heavy stars are like extravagant spenders: they burn through their hydrogen so quickly that they may last only a few million years. Small red stars are thrifty by comparison, sipping their fuel so slowly that they could shine for trillions of years, far longer than the present age of the Universe. Our Sun lies somewhere in between, and it will last about ten billion years in all.

As a large star ages and runs short of hydrogen, its core shrinks and heats up until helium itself can be fused into carbon and oxygen. The biggest stars go much further, building neon, silicon and other elements in layers, so that a dying giant is arranged rather like an onion, with the heaviest atoms at its centre. In this way stars act as the factories for most of the elements that are not hydrogen or helium.

Iron is the end of the line, because fusing it takes in energy instead of giving energy out. When a giant star's core turns to iron, the outward push disappears, the core collapses in a fraction of a second, and the outer layers are blown apart. This explosion is called a supernova, and for a few weeks a single dying star can shine as brightly as a whole galaxy.

A supernova throws the carbon, oxygen and iron from a star's layers out into space. Heavier metals, such as gold, need even more violent events, and in 2017 astronomers watched two neutron stars collide and found signs that the crash had forged gold and other heavy elements. Scientists think other rare events may also make some of these metals, and they are still working out how much comes from each.

The hydrogen in your body is nearly as old as the Universe, because it was made in the Big Bang. Almost everything else, including the carbon in your cells, the calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood, was cooked inside stars that lived and died before the Sun was born. In a very real sense you are made of stardust, recycled through many generations of stars.

Gravity did not stop with single stars, but went on gathering them into vast communities called galaxies. Each one holds millions or billions of stars, together with gas, dust and a great deal of unseen matter. Young galaxies often collided and merged, so the large ones we see today were built up from many smaller pieces.

Astronomers sort galaxies into three broad shapes, each with its own name and its own history. Spirals have graceful curving arms that wind around a bright centre like a whirlpool, ellipticals are smooth, rounded balls of old stars, and irregular galaxies have no tidy form at all. The shape often tells a story, because collisions tend to wreck spirals and leave round, quiet ellipticals behind.

Our home galaxy is the Milky Way, a spiral of a few hundred billion stars that measures about a hundred thousand light years across. The Sun sits in a quiet outer region, roughly twenty-six thousand light years from the centre, in a minor arm of the spiral. Seen from above, we would be a single faint point somewhere in the suburbs.

The Sun is not standing still, but sweeping around the centre of the Milky Way at more than two hundred kilometres every second. Even at that speed, one full orbit takes roughly two hundred and thirty million years. The last time we were in this part of our journey, the first dinosaurs were just beginning to appear on Earth.

On a dark night far from the city, a pale band of light arches over the sky, and that band is the Milky Way. You are looking edge-on along the flat disc of your own galaxy from the inside, so its countless stars blend into a single misty glow. A great many people have never seen it, because the glare of streetlights hides it from most towns and cities.

A black hole is a region where matter has been crushed so tightly that its gravity does not let even light escape. Many of them form when a very heavy star collapses at the end of its life, leaving its matter squeezed into a tiny space. At the centre of the Milky Way lies a giant one, about four million times as heavy as the Sun, and astronomers have tracked stars whirling around it.

The Andromeda galaxy lies about two and a half million light years away and is drifting slowly toward us. Astronomers expect that the two galaxies may merge in several billion years, though recent studies suggest the collision is far from certain. Even if it happens, the stars are spread so thinly that very few would actually hit one another.

Stars in the outer parts of a galaxy orbit much faster than the gravity of all the visible matter should allow. Astronomers therefore conclude that galaxies are wrapped in a vast halo of invisible material that they call dark matter. It does not give out or block light, and we know it only through its gravity, so its real nature is still unknown.

Gravity should be slowing the expansion of the Universe, so astronomers were astonished in the late 1990s when distant exploding stars showed that it is actually speeding up. They gave the unknown cause the name dark energy, which describes our ignorance better than it explains anything. Whether it is a property of empty space or something else entirely is one of the biggest open questions in science.

Everything you can see, from your own hand to the farthest galaxy, is made of ordinary matter, and that adds up to only about five per cent of the Universe. Roughly a quarter is dark matter and almost seventy per cent is dark energy, and neither has yet been explained. It is a humbling thought that most of the cosmos remains a mystery, and that the mystery is still waiting to be solved.

About four and a half billion years ago, a cloud of gas and dust, left over from earlier stars, began to collapse under its own weight. Something may have nudged it, perhaps the shock wave from a nearby supernova, though that is still debated. As it shrank, its middle grew dense and hot while the rest swirled around it.

As the cloud shrank it spun faster, in the way that a skater turns more quickly when she pulls in her arms. Its matter flattened into a wide disc, and almost all of it, more than ninety-nine per cent, fell inwards to form the young Sun. What remained in the disc was a thin layer of dust and gas, and from that the planets would be built.

Within the disc, microscopic grains of dust clung together and grew into pebbles, then boulders, then lumps the size of mountains. Once those lumps were large enough, their own gravity swept up whatever lay in their path, and violent collisions built them into planets over tens of millions of years. The process was messy, and the early Solar System was a crowded and dangerous place.

Close to the hot young Sun, only rock and metal could remain solid, so the four inner planets ended up small and rocky. Farther out it was cold enough for ice to form as well, and the giant planets there grew heavy enough to capture thick coats of hydrogen and helium. That is why the Solar System has two very different kinds of world, divided by a line that astronomers call the frost line.

The Sun is a ball of hot gas about one hundred and nine times wider than the Earth, and more than a million Earths could fit inside it. Yet among the stars it is quite ordinary, neither especially large nor especially small. It is about halfway through its life, with roughly five billion years of steady shining still to come.

Mercury, the smallest planet, has almost no air to hold the heat, so its days are scorching and its nights bitterly cold. Venus is hotter still, because a thick blanket of carbon dioxide traps the Sun's warmth and holds its surface at about four hundred and sixty degrees Celsius. It is the hottest planet in the Solar System, even though Mercury is much closer to the Sun, and it makes a fierce warning about the greenhouse effect.

Mars looks red because its rocks and dust contain iron that has rusted, just like an old nail left out in the rain. Billions of years ago, rivers ran across its surface and lakes filled its craters, as robot explorers have shown from the rocks they have studied. Today the planet is cold and dry, with air too thin to hold much heat, and most of its water is frozen at the poles or beneath the ground.

Jupiter is the giant of the Solar System, more than twice as heavy as all the other planets put together, and it is made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than the entire Earth, and it has been seen swirling for centuries. Jupiter also has dozens of moons, and one of them, Europa, hides a deep ocean of liquid water beneath its icy shell.

Saturn's famous rings are made of countless pieces of ice, from tiny grains to lumps as big as houses, spread out in a disc that is very wide and astonishingly thin. Far beyond it, Uranus and Neptune are cold blue giants, made largely of water, ammonia and methane. Winds on Neptune blow faster than any hurricane on Earth, even though the planet receives very little warmth from the Sun.

Beyond Neptune lies a vast, frozen zone of icy bodies, among them the dwarf planet Pluto, which astronomers stopped calling a full planet in 2006. Comets are lumps of ice and dust that fall inwards from this region, and perhaps from a far larger cloud that scientists think surrounds the Solar System but nobody has seen. The two Voyager spacecraft, launched in 1977, have now left the Sun's neighbourhood and are the most distant objects that people have made.

The infant Earth was assembled from countless collisions, and every impact released a great deal of heat. For a long time its surface was a glowing sea of melted rock, with no oceans, no solid ground and certainly no life. Many scientists call this earliest age the Hadean, a name borrowed from the underworld of Greek myth.

While the Earth was still molten, its heaviest materials, mostly iron and nickel, sank towards the centre under their own weight. Lighter rock floated above them, much as oil rises over water, and the planet sorted itself into layers. That sorting is the reason we have a metal core, a thick middle layer and a thin outer crust.

The leading explanation for the Moon is that a world about the size of Mars slammed into the young Earth, and astronomers have given the intruder the name Theia. The collision threw a huge cloud of melted rock into orbit, and within a surprisingly short time that cloud gathered itself into the Moon. It remains a theory, but it explains many facts that older ideas could not.

Between 1969 and 1972, the Apollo astronauts carried home about three hundred and eighty kilograms of rock from the Moon. When scientists studied it, they found that it was chemically very similar to the rock in the Earth's outer layers, as if the two worlds shared a common origin. That match is one of the strongest clues that the Moon was born in a great collision.

The Moon spins once on its axis in exactly the time that it takes to circle the Earth once. As a result, it always turns the same face towards us, and the far side can be seen only from spacecraft. This is no coincidence, because the Earth's gravity gradually slowed the Moon's spin until the two movements matched.

The gravity of the Moon pulls hardest on the side of the Earth that faces it, and the oceans there swell into a gentle bulge. A second bulge forms on the opposite side, so as the Earth turns, most coasts experience two high tides and two low tides each day. The Sun also pulls on the sea, and when it lines up with the Moon the tides grow especially strong.

Astronauts left mirrors on the Moon, and scientists on Earth bounce laser beams off them to measure the distance very precisely. They have found that the Moon is drifting away from us by about four centimetres every year, roughly as fast as a fingernail grows. Long ago it was much closer, and it would have looked enormous in the sky of the young Earth.

The Earth leans over by about twenty-three degrees, and that lean is the reason we have summer and winter. Many scientists think that the Moon's gravity acts like a gentle hand, keeping the lean from wobbling wildly over long ages. If so, the Moon has helped to keep our climate steady enough for life to flourish, although this idea is still debated.

Some atoms are unstable and change slowly into other kinds of atom, at a rate that never varies, and the process is known as radioactive decay. By measuring how much of a rock has already changed, scientists can tell how long ago it formed. The oldest meteorites are about four and a half billion years old, and careful calculations for the Earth itself give nearly the same result.

The oldest known pieces of the young Earth are microscopic crystals of a mineral called zircon, found in the rocks of Western Australia. They are nearly four and a half billion years old, and their chemistry hints that the planet already had a solid crust and perhaps even liquid water. That would mean the early Earth cooled much sooner than people once believed, although scientists still argue about how to read the evidence.

The Earth is built in layers: a thin crust, a thick mantle of hot rock, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core made of iron and nickel. The deepest hole that people have ever drilled reaches only about twelve kilometres, which barely scratches the surface of a planet whose centre lies more than six thousand kilometres down. Almost everything we know about the layers below has therefore been learned without ever going there.

When a big earthquake strikes, waves of shaking race through the whole planet and are picked up by instruments all over the world. By studying how they speed up, bend and sometimes vanish, scientists have drawn a map of the deep inside. One kind of wave cannot cross liquid, and that is how they discovered that the outer core is molten.

The inner core is a ball of iron and nickel a little smaller than the Moon, and it is about as hot as the surface of the Sun. It stays solid in spite of that heat, because the pressure at the centre of the Earth is crushing enough to hold the atoms rigidly in place. Around it, the liquid outer core slowly churns, and that motion is the source of the planet's magnetic field.

The mantle is made of solid rock, yet over millions of years it behaves like a thick, slow-moving syrup. Hot rock rises from deep below, cools near the top and sinks again, in great loops that take tens of millions of years to complete. This slow stirring drags on the crust above, and it is the engine behind almost everything that moves on the surface.

The crust is not one unbroken shell but a jigsaw of several huge plates and many smaller ones, like the pieces of a cracked eggshell. Each plate carries continents or ocean floor on its back, and they creep across the planet at only a few centimetres a year. That is far too slow to notice, yet over millions of years it is enough to rearrange the whole map.

Plates meet in three ways: they can pull apart, push together, or grind sideways past one another, and each kind of meeting builds something different. Where they separate, new crust forms from rising hot rock, and where they collide, one plate may dive beneath the other or both may crumple upwards. Most of the world's earthquakes and volcanoes happen along these edges, so the boundaries can be traced on a map by the shaking and the fire alone.

The edges of plates are rough, so they tend to catch on one another instead of gliding smoothly. Stress builds up in the rock for years or even centuries, until at last it slips along a crack called a fault, and the sudden release shakes the ground. Scientists can map where earthquakes are likely, but they still cannot predict exactly when one will strike.

A volcano forms wherever melted rock, called magma, finds a path to the surface and bursts out as lava, ash and gas. Roughly three quarters of the world's active volcanoes lie in a great horseshoe around the Pacific Ocean, a region that is known as the Ring of Fire. Eruptions can be destructive, but over long ages they have also built islands, enriched soil and released the gases that made the air and seas.

About fifty million years ago, the plate carrying India collided with the rest of Asia, and the crust between them crumpled upwards into the Himalayas. The collision is still going on, and the mountains are rising by a few millimetres every year. Near the summit of Mount Everest there are rocks that hold the fossils of sea creatures, proof that the highest place on land was once at the bottom of an ocean.

About three hundred million years ago, nearly all the land on Earth was joined together in a single supercontinent that we call Pangaea. In 1912 the German scientist Alfred Wegener argued that the continents drift, pointing out how neatly South America and Africa fit together, but most experts rejected him because he could not explain the force. Only in the 1960s, when evidence showed that new crust was forming on the sea floor, did his central idea win the argument.

The air that you are breathing is about seventy-eight per cent nitrogen and twenty-one per cent oxygen. Nearly all of the remaining one per cent is a gas called argon, with only tiny amounts of carbon dioxide, water vapour and other gases. Small as those traces are, they have an outsized influence on the weather and the climate.

The atmosphere feels limitless, but it is really a thin skin: half of all its air lies within about five and a half kilometres of the ground. Climbers on the summit of Mount Everest, nearly nine kilometres up, find so little oxygen that most of them need a mask to breathe. There is no sharp edge to the sky, but space is usually said to begin about a hundred kilometres up.

Oceans cover about seventy per cent of the Earth's surface, which is why the planet looks blue from space. Where all that water came from is still debated, and the main suggestions are comets, watery asteroids and the young Earth's own rocks, which may have released it. Studies of meteorites show that many asteroids carry water that is chemically very like our own, which makes them strong suspects.

Most solids sink in their own liquid, but ice floats on water, because water expands slightly as it freezes. A frozen lake therefore forms a lid at the top, and the water beneath it stays liquid, so fish and other creatures can survive the winter. This small oddity of water has helped life to continue through the coldest ages of Earth's history.

Sunlight warms the oceans and lifts water into the air as an invisible vapour, which cools high up and gathers into clouds. The water then falls as rain or snow, runs down rivers and returns to the sea, ready to begin the journey again. Nothing is made or lost along the way, so the water in your glass has been circling the planet for billions of years and may once have fallen on a dinosaur.

The Sun does not warm the planet evenly, because the tropics receive far more sunlight than the poles do, and land warms faster than sea. Warm air rises, cooler air flows in to take its place, and that endless movement is what we call wind. Add the spin of the Earth and the water in the air, and you have the ever-changing pattern that we call weather.

Certain gases in the air, including carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour, let sunlight pass through but slow down the heat trying to escape back to space. This greenhouse effect is entirely natural and essential, because without it the average temperature of the Earth would be about thirty degrees colder, and most of the water would be frozen. The real question is not whether this blanket exists, but how thick it is becoming.

Carbon moves in a vast cycle through the air, living things, the oceans and the rocks, with plants taking it in and animals, fires and decay giving it back. Coal, oil and gas are the buried remains of ancient life, and burning them releases carbon that was locked away for hundreds of millions of years. We are returning it to the air far faster than natural processes can take it out again.

Before the age of factories, the air held about two hundred and eighty parts of carbon dioxide in every million, and today it holds more than four hundred and twenty. Over the same period, the average temperature of the Earth's surface has risen by a little more than one degree Celsius. That may sound small, but averaged over a whole planet it represents an enormous amount of extra heat.

Deep in Antarctica, scientists drill long cores of ice that hold tiny bubbles of air trapped up to eight hundred thousand years ago. They show that ice ages and warm periods rose and fell along with carbon dioxide, and that today's level is higher than at any time in the entire record. Together with thermometers, melting glaciers and seas that have risen by about twenty centimetres since 1900, this is why nearly all climate scientists agree that people are the main cause of today's warming.

Mud and sand settle in layers, and in an undisturbed cliff the lowest layers are usually the oldest. Fossils, which are the remains or traces of ancient living things, are found inside these layers, and they reveal which creatures lived at which time. Read together, the layers and the fossils form a kind of library whose pages span millions of years.

Imagine the whole history of the Earth squeezed into a single calendar year, with the planet forming at midnight on the first of January. Life appears by about March, the dinosaurs disappear on the day after Christmas, and modern people arrive only in the last forty minutes of New Year's Eve. All of written history would fit into the last half minute before the new year begins.

Defining life turns out to be surprisingly hard, and scientists still argue over the exact words. Most agree that living things use energy, grow, respond to their surroundings and make copies of themselves, and that over many generations their descendants change. By that test a rock fails completely, while a candle flame passes only part of it, which shows why the boundary is a little blurry.

In 1953, a young chemist filled a glass flask with water and simple gases, then sent electric sparks through it to imitate lightning on the early Earth. Within days the water had turned brown and was full of amino acids, which are the building blocks of the proteins found in all living things. The result showed that the ingredients of life can form easily, although it did not explain how they became alive.

Some scientists suspect that life began in warm, shallow pools that dried and filled again, while others point to hot vents on the sea floor, where minerals and heat pour out of the rock. A few have suggested that clay surfaces gathered the first chemicals and helped them to react. Each idea has strengths and weaknesses, and none has been proved, so the origin of life remains an open question.

Among the oldest signs of life are layered mounds called stromatolites, built by microbes in rocks from Western Australia that are about three and a half billion years old. Some chemical traces in even older rock may also come from living things, but experts still argue about whether they are real. Either way, life arrived early, and it has been present for most of the history of the planet.

A cell is a collection of chemicals wrapped in a thin, oily skin, and it is the smallest unit that can be called alive. The first cells were very simple, and for billions of years every living thing on Earth consisted of just one of them. Even today, most of the living things on our planet are single cells, far too small for the eye to see.

In 1665 the English scientist Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork through a microscope and called the tiny boxes that he saw cells, because they reminded him of small rooms. Scientists now estimate that a human body is made of about thirty-seven trillion cells, of many different kinds. Each one is a busy living factory, yet most are far smaller than the full stop at the end of this sentence.

Inside almost every cell lies DNA, a very long molecule in the shape of a twisted ladder, and it carries the instructions for building and running a living thing. The instructions are written in a code of four chemical letters, and the human set of them holds about three billion pairs. Scientists worked out the shape of DNA in 1953, helped by the X-ray pictures that Rosalind Franklin had taken.

A gene is a stretch of DNA that holds the recipe for a particular protein, and proteins do most of the work inside a living cell. You inherited half of your genes from each parent, and about twenty thousand genes make up the instructions for a human being. Whenever DNA is copied, rare mistakes called mutations creep in, and these tiny changes are the raw material from which new variety arises.

In 1831 a young Englishman called Charles Darwin boarded the ship Beagle for a voyage round the world that lasted almost five years. He collected plants, animals and fossils everywhere he landed, and he was struck by how closely related creatures differed from one island or coast to the next. Those observations lodged in his mind, and he spent more than twenty years turning them over before he published his famous book.

Darwin's idea of natural selection rests on three simple observations about the living world. Individuals of any kind vary a little, more are born than can survive, and those whose features suit their surroundings are more likely to survive, breed and pass those features on. Repeated for countless generations, this slow filtering can change a whole population and even divide it into new species.

On the Galapagos Islands there are finches whose beaks range from thick and strong, for cracking seeds, to slender and sharp, for catching insects. Scientists who measured the birds year after year found that the average beak grew deeper after a drought, because only the sturdiest beaks could crack the few hard seeds that were left. Evolution, it turns out, can sometimes be seen happening within the span of a single human lifetime.

When an antibiotic kills most of the bacteria in a patient, any that happen to resist the drug survive and multiply, and their offspring inherit that resistance. Over the years this process has produced germs that few medicines can touch, and it is natural selection happening before our eyes in hospitals and on farms. For that reason doctors are asked to use these drugs only when they are really needed.

Dogs are descended from wolves, and over many thousands of years people have shaped them by choosing which animals were allowed to breed. From that steady selection came the tiny Chihuahua and the towering Great Dane, along with hundreds of other breeds that all belong to a single species. Natural selection works in the same way, except that nature, rather than a breeder, does the choosing.

In the 1860s, a monk named Gregor Mendel grew thousands of pea plants in his monastery garden, carefully counting the tall and short, the yellow and green. He found that features are handed down in separate units, which we now call genes, and that some can hide for a generation before they reappear. His paper was almost ignored in his lifetime, and its importance was recognised only around the year 1900.

Mutations occur by chance, yet natural selection is not chance at all, because the environment steadily favours the features that help survival. Evolution has no goal and no plan, and it never aims at humans or at any other final result. It does not make creatures better in some absolute sense, only better suited to the place and time in which they live.

Fossils show how whole groups of animals changed over time, and sometimes they fill a gap that scientists had expected to find. Tiktaalik, a fish about three hundred and seventy-five million years old, had strong fins that could prop up its body and a neck that could turn, like early land animals. Scientists chose rocks of the right age to search, and they found it in Arctic Canada in 2004.

Comparing the DNA of different species is rather like comparing family records, and the pattern is clear. Humans share about ninety-eight per cent of the matching parts of their DNA with chimpanzees, many genes with mice, and even some with yeast and plants. All life uses the same genetic code, which points to a single ancestor, sometimes called LUCA, that lived more than three and a half billion years ago.

In everyday speech a theory is just a guess, but in science it means a well-tested explanation that fits a large body of evidence. Evolution is a theory in that strong sense, in the same way that gravity and the atomic theory are. Fossils, DNA and direct observation all support it, and new discoveries have added to its strength rather than overturning it.

Cyanobacteria are microscopic living things that can use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make their own food, in a process called photosynthesis. As a waste product they release oxygen, and they have been doing so for well over two billion years. Plants still make food in the same way today, using tiny green parts that descend from ancient cyanobacteria.

At first, the oxygen reacted with iron dissolved in the sea, turning it to rust that settled on the sea floor in red and grey bands which we can still see in rocks today. When the iron was used up, about two and a half billion years ago, free oxygen began to build up in the air. This Great Oxidation Event was a disaster for many microbes, because oxygen was poisonous to them, but it opened the way for much more energetic forms of life.

The cells of animals, plants and fungi are far more complex than bacteria, with a nucleus that holds the DNA and tiny power stations called mitochondria. Many scientists believe that mitochondria began as free-living bacteria that were swallowed by another cell and never digested, so that the two settled into a partnership. Mitochondria still carry a little DNA of their own, which is one of the best clues that this strange story is true.

For about three billion years, nearly all life on Earth stayed microscopic, drifting and dividing in the sea. Then, in several different groups, cells began to stick together and share the work, with some specialising in feeding, some in moving and some in reproducing. Many-celled life seems to have arisen on more than one occasion, which suggests that it was not such a difficult step as scientists once imagined.

Between about five hundred and seventy and five hundred and forty million years ago, the sea floor was home to strange, soft-bodied creatures that we call the Ediacaran life. Some looked like fronds or quilted mats, and most had no shells, claws or obvious mouths. Scientists are still debating how they are related to the animals that came afterwards, and a few may belong to groups that have long since vanished.

About five hundred and forty million years ago the Cambrian period began, and the fossil record suddenly fills with animals that have shells, spines, legs and claws. Within some twenty million years, nearly all the main groups of animals alive today had appeared, a burst that is called the Cambrian explosion. It was not an explosion in the everyday sense, since twenty million years is a long time, but in the history of life it was remarkably quick.

The Cambrian sea held fierce hunters, armoured trilobites and some of the first animals with sharp, complex eyes, which began an arms race between hunter and hunted. We know a great deal about them because of the Burgess Shale in Canada, where fine mud buried creatures so gently that even their soft parts were preserved. One hunter there, Anomalocaris, was perhaps half a metre long and had a pair of spiny grasping arms.

Among the early animals were small fish-like creatures, and by about five hundred million years ago some of them had a stiff rod along their backs that became the backbone. Later, some fish developed hinged jaws from the bones that had held up their gills, and with those jaws they became the most powerful hunters of the sea. Every animal with a backbone alive today, including you, descends from those early swimmers.

About four hundred and seventy million years ago, small plants a little like mosses began to creep out of the water and onto the bare land. Working together with fungi, they helped to break down the rock and gradually build the first real soil, which allowed taller plants to follow. Before then the land had been almost bare, with only thin films of microbes here and there.

Small relatives of insects, spiders and millipedes were probably the first animals to settle on land, some four hundred and thirty million years ago. Later, some fish with strong, jointed fins began to spend time out of the water, and within a few tens of millions of years they had become four-legged animals that could walk. Every amphibian, reptile, bird and mammal, including you, descends from those first backboned visitors to the shore.

About three hundred million years ago, warm, wet forests of giant ferns, club mosses and early trees covered much of the land. When their dead wood sank into swamps and was buried, it slowly turned to coal, which is why so much of our coal dates from that age. Among the trunks flew dragonfly-like insects with wings as wide as a pigeon's, helped by air that held more oxygen than ours does today.

About two hundred and fifty-two million years ago came the worst mass extinction in the history of life, sometimes called the Great Dying. Scientists think that enormous volcanic eruptions in Siberia poured out so much carbon dioxide and other gases that the air and the oceans changed, and most of the species on Earth disappeared. Life survived, but it took millions of years for the world to recover from the blow.

Scientists recognise five great mass extinctions in the history of life, each of which swept away a large share of the world's species. Their causes included volcanoes, changes in climate and ocean chemistry, and, in one case, an asteroid. Yet after every disaster the survivors spread into the empty places they left behind, and the story of life continued in new directions.

After the Great Dying, reptiles of many kinds spread to fill the empty land. The first dinosaurs appeared about two hundred and thirty million years ago, and they were small, quick animals that ran on two legs. For a while they were just one group among many, and they became the rulers of the land only after a later extinction cleared away some of their rivals.

The largest long-necked dinosaurs were among the heaviest animals ever to walk on land, and some weighed more than ten elephants. Others were no bigger than a chicken, and fossils found in China since the 1990s show that many of these smaller kinds were covered in feathers. Dinosaurs were not a single kind of animal but a huge and varied family that lived in almost every habitat on land.

About a hundred and fifty million years ago, Archaeopteryx, a creature about the size of a magpie, had feathered wings, sharp teeth and a long bony tail. Scientists now agree that birds descend from small feathered dinosaurs, which means that the dinosaurs never entirely died out. The sparrow on your window sill and the chicken on your plate are living members of that ancient family.

Tyrannosaurus rex was a hunter about twelve metres long, with jaws strong enough to crush bone. It lived only about sixty-six to sixty-eight million years ago, which means it is separated from us by less time than it is from Stegosaurus, an earlier plated dinosaur. The age of the dinosaurs was so long that creatures we picture as neighbours were separated by tens of millions of years.

Reptiles also ruled the seas and the skies, but those great swimmers and flyers were not dinosaurs. Plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs hunted in the water, while pterosaurs, the first backboned animals ever to fly, soared overhead on wings of stretched skin. The largest pterosaurs had a wingspan about as wide as that of a small aeroplane.

About sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid roughly ten kilometres wide struck the sea near what is now the coast of Mexico. It left a crater about a hundred and eighty kilometres across, and the impact threw so much dust and burning rock into the air that the whole world was changed. Sunlight was dimmed, plants struggled and food chains broke apart, and within a short time about three quarters of all species had died.

In 1980 a team of scientists found a thin layer of clay in rocks from that very time, rich in a metal called iridium. Iridium is rare at the Earth's surface but common in asteroids, and the same layer was soon found at sites all over the world. Later the crater itself was found, and today almost everyone agrees that the impact ended the age of dinosaurs, although huge volcanic eruptions may have added to the harm.

Mammals had lived alongside the dinosaurs for well over a hundred million years, but they were mostly small creatures that hid in burrows and hunted at night. After the asteroid, many of them survived, perhaps because small animals needed less food and could shelter underground. The empty world that followed gave them room to grow, and within some ten million years they had spread into a huge variety of shapes and sizes.

About fifty million years ago, the ancestors of whales were four-legged animals that walked on land and waded into rivers and shallows. Fossils from India and Pakistan show their legs shrinking and their bodies becoming sleeker over millions of years. The closest living relatives of whales turn out to be hippopotamuses, a surprising result that DNA and fossils both support.

The first primates, the group that includes monkeys, apes and humans, appeared more than fifty million years ago. They lived in trees, and they developed grasping hands, forward-facing eyes that judge distance well, and brains that were large for their size. Meanwhile, as the world cooled, grasslands spread, and in time horses, antelopes and many other grazing animals found a home on them.

Humans are apes, and our closest living relatives are the chimpanzees and the bonobos. We are not descended from them, which is a common mistake, for both they and we descend from an ancestor that lived about six to seven million years ago. Since then, each line has changed, and our line took the path that led to upright walking and big brains.

In 1974, scientists in Ethiopia discovered the bones of an early human relative that they nicknamed Lucy, who lived about three million years ago. She stood only about one metre tall and had a small, ape-sized brain, yet the shape of her legs and hips shows that she walked upright. Footprints of similar creatures, left in volcanic ash in Tanzania, confirm that our ancestors were walking on two feet long before they had big brains.

Early members of our own genus, Homo, were making sharp stone tools for cutting meat and plants about two and a half million years ago. They also learned to use fire, at least a million years ago, which gave them warmth, protection from hunters and cooked food that is easier to digest. Some scientists think the energy from cooked food helped human brains to grow, although that idea is still debated.

Homo erectus, a tall and athletic human with a larger brain than Lucy's, appeared nearly two million years ago. Members of this species were the first humans to leave Africa, and their fossils have been found in places as far apart as Georgia and Indonesia. They survived for well over a million years, much longer than our own species has so far.

Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia for hundreds of thousands of years, and they made tools, controlled fire and cared for their injured. They died out about forty thousand years ago, but they left a trace behind, because most people outside Africa carry one or two per cent of Neanderthal DNA. This shows that some of our own ancestors met the Neanderthals and had children with them.

Our own species, Homo sapiens, appeared in Africa about three hundred thousand years ago, and the oldest known fossils come from Morocco. Beginning perhaps seventy thousand years ago, some groups spread out into Asia, Europe and Australia, and later the Americas, until people lived on every continent except Antarctica. Every one of the eight billion of us alive today descends from those travellers.

Farming began about eleven thousand years ago, and the first cities and the first writing appeared roughly five thousand years ago. Measured against the history of the Earth, that is less than the blink of an eye, yet almost everything that we call human history took place within it. From the pyramids to the telescope, every book ever written belongs to this tiny final slice of time.

Microbes are living things too small to see without a microscope, and they live everywhere: in soil, in sea water, in the air and on your skin. A human body carries roughly as many bacterial cells as human ones, most of them in the gut. For most of Earth's history microbes were the only life there was, and in many ways they still run the planet.

Only a small fraction of all the microbes in the world ever cause illness. Many of those in your gut help to break down food, some make vitamins that your body needs, and others help to train your defences against harmful germs. Microbes also make bread rise and turn milk into yoghurt, so people have been using them for thousands of years without knowing.

For centuries people blamed bad air, bad luck or the anger of the gods for disease. In the 1800s, scientists such as Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch showed by careful experiments that particular germs cause particular illnesses. This germ theory is one of the most important ideas in the history of medicine, because once the enemy had been identified, people could start to fight it.

In 1847 a doctor in Vienna named Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that far fewer new mothers died when doctors washed their hands in a strong cleaning liquid before helping at births. Many of his colleagues refused to believe him, because germs had not yet been discovered and nobody could say why it worked. Today, washing hands is still one of the cheapest and most effective ways of preventing disease.

In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner showed that infection with a mild disease called cowpox could protect a person from the deadly smallpox. Vaccination spread around the world, and in 1980 the World Health Organization declared that smallpox had been wiped out, the only human disease so far to disappear completely. Before that, it had killed hundreds of millions of people in the twentieth century alone.

Your immune system is a team of cells and proteins that finds and destroys invaders. A vaccine shows that team a harmless piece or weakened copy of a germ in advance, so that it remembers the enemy and can respond quickly if the real one ever arrives. In this way a vaccine gives the protection that an illness would give, without the illness itself.

In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from a holiday and noticed that a mould had killed the bacteria growing around it in a forgotten dish. Some years later, other scientists worked out how to make large amounts of its chemical, penicillin, and it became the first widely used antibiotic. Antibiotics have saved countless lives, but bacteria are evolving resistance, which means that new medicines are always needed.

A virus is a tiny package of genes wrapped in a coat of protein, and it is far smaller than even a bacterium. It cannot grow or copy itself alone, so it slips inside a living cell and uses the cell's machinery to make thousands of new viruses. Because of this, scientists still argue about whether viruses should be called alive, and antibiotics, which work on bacteria, have no effect on them.

In 1854 a London doctor named John Snow marked on a map the homes of people who had died of cholera, and he found that they clustered around a single water pump. When the handle of the pump was removed, the outbreak faded, and in time cities built sewers and clean water supplies to prevent such disasters. These plain pipes and drains have probably saved more lives than most of the dramatic medicines that followed them.

In 1800, the average person in the world could expect to live only about thirty to thirty-five years, largely because so many children died young. Today the global average is over seventy, thanks to better food, clean water, vaccines, antibiotics and safer childbirth. Science did not make us immortal, but it has more than doubled the time that most of us can expect to enjoy.

Nearly twenty-five centuries ago, the Greek thinker Democritus argued that if you could cut a stone again and again, you would at last reach a piece too small to divide. He called it an atom, a word that means uncuttable, but he had no way to test the idea and many people ignored it. Real evidence arrived only in the nineteenth century, when chemists noticed that substances always combine in fixed amounts.

Atoms are almost too small for the human mind to picture, and quite impossible to see. A single human hair is about half a million atoms wide, and the dot over a letter i holds trillions of them. Even the best light microscopes cannot show one, and pictures of single atoms were made only in the twentieth century, with special instruments.

At the centre of every atom lies a tiny nucleus, made of positively charged protons and uncharged neutrons. Around it move electrons, which carry negative charge and are almost two thousand times lighter than a proton. The attraction between the positive and negative charges is what holds an atom together.

If an atom were as large as a football stadium, its nucleus would be a grain of sand at the centre, and the electrons would be specks whirling far out in the stands. In 1911 Ernest Rutherford discovered this by firing tiny particles at a sheet of gold foil, and nearly all of them passed straight through. A few bounced back sharply, which could only mean that nearly all of the mass of an atom is packed into a very small core.

An element is a single kind of atom, and what makes it what it is, is the number of protons in its nucleus. Hydrogen has only one, carbon has six, oxygen has eight, and gold, which is far heavier, has seventy-nine. Change the number of protons and you change the element, which is why turning lead into gold, the old dream of the alchemists, could never be done by ordinary chemistry.

In 1869 the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements then known in a table, so that those with similar behaviour fell into the same column. He left gaps where he thought undiscovered elements belonged, and he even predicted what they would be like, and when they were found he was proved right. Today the periodic table holds one hundred and eighteen elements, about ninety of which occur naturally on Earth.

Atoms stick together by sharing or swapping their outermost electrons, and groups of joined atoms are called molecules. When two hydrogen atoms bond with one oxygen atom, they make a molecule of water, which behaves quite unlike either of the gases from which it is made. Everything you can touch, from salt to silk, owes its properties to the way its atoms are joined.

When a candle burns, it seems to vanish into thin air, but that is only an illusion. Its carbon and hydrogen atoms combine with oxygen from the air and drift away as carbon dioxide and water vapour, and if you could weigh everything, the total would be unchanged. In the late 1700s the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier showed that matter is rearranged in a chemical reaction but never destroyed.

Some atoms have nuclei that are unstable, and sooner or later they break apart, giving out energy as radiation and changing into a different element. The scientist Marie Curie studied this radioactivity around the year 1900, and she was the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Today the same process is used to date ancient rocks, to power spacecraft and to make pictures of the inside of the body.

Atoms are never consumed or destroyed, and they are merely shuffled from one place to another. The carbon in your body has travelled through the air, the soil, the leaves of plants and probably the bodies of many other living creatures before it reached you. Over the years most of the atoms in you are replaced, yet you remain yourself, because what matters is the pattern rather than the particular atoms.

Energy is the ability to make things change, whether that means moving, warming, shining or growing. It comes in many forms, including the energy of movement, of heat, of light and of sound, and the energy stored in food, fuel and batteries. Nothing at all happens in the Universe without energy changing from one form into another.

When you throw a ball, the stored energy in your muscles becomes the movement of the ball, and when it lands that movement turns into a little heat and sound. If you add up all the energy before and after, the total is always the same, and this rule, called the conservation of energy, has never been broken in any experiment. Energy is never made or destroyed, but only moved around from place to place and changed.

Heat is the energy of atoms and molecules jiggling and bumping about, and temperature is a measure of how fast they move on average. The faster they move, the hotter something feels, and the slower they move, the colder it becomes. There is a lowest possible temperature, called absolute zero, at about minus two hundred and seventy-three degrees Celsius, where almost all of this motion stops.

Heat flows from hot things to cold things and never the other way round without help, which is why your tea cools down but never warms itself up. Scientists describe this with the idea of entropy, a measure of how spread out and disordered energy has become, and it tends to increase. That one-way trend is one reason why time seems to flow in a single direction, from past to future.

The food that you eat holds chemical energy, and nearly all of it was first captured from sunlight by plants. Inside your cells, the mitochondria use oxygen to release that energy slowly, in many small steps, and store it in a molecule that works like a rechargeable battery. Some of the energy is lost as heat, which is why your body stays warm at about thirty-seven degrees Celsius.

In 1687 the English scientist Isaac Newton published the laws that describe how things move. His first law says that an object stays at rest, or keeps travelling in a straight line at a steady speed, unless a force acts on it. This was a surprise, because on Earth things always seem to slow down, and the true reason is that friction and air push against them.

Newton's second law says that the harder you push something, the more quickly its motion changes, and the heavier it is, the less it changes for the same push. That is why an empty shopping trolley is easy to start and a full one is not. Engineers use this simple rule every day, to design everything from bicycles to aeroplanes.

Newton's third law says that when one object pushes on another, the second object pushes back with an equal force in the opposite direction. A swimmer moves forward by pushing the water backward, and a rocket rises because it throws hot gas downward and the gas pushes it up. Rockets even work in the emptiness of space, because they need no air to push against, only the gas they carry.

Friction is the force that resists when two surfaces rub against each other, and it turns movement into heat. It slows a sliding box and wears out the soles of your shoes, yet life without it would be impossible, because you could not walk, grip a pencil or tie a knot. Even ice, which is slippery, gives some friction, and that is why a skater can push off from it.

In 1905 Albert Einstein realised that mass is a very concentrated form of energy, and his famous equation tells us exactly how much. Because the speed of light is so enormous, even a tiny amount of matter can release a huge amount of energy. Every second, the Sun turns about four million tonnes of its own matter into light and heat, and it has been doing so for billions of years.

A wave carries energy from place to place without carrying the water or the air along with it, as you can see when a ripple crosses a pond and a floating leaf only bobs up and down. Sound is a wave of squeezed and stretched air, and it travels at about three hundred and forty metres every second. Light travels almost a million times faster, which is why you see lightning first and hear the thunder afterwards.

In the 1660s Isaac Newton passed a narrow beam of sunlight through a glass prism and saw it spread into a band of colours, from red to violet. He showed that white light is really a mixture of all of them, and that the prism had only separated what was already there. A rainbow forms in just the same way, when millions of raindrops bend and split the sunlight that enters them.

The colours that your eyes can see are only a narrow slice of a much larger family of waves. Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet light, X-rays and gamma rays are all the same kind of wave, differing only in how long each wave is. Every one of them travels at the speed of light through empty space, and astronomers use all of them to study the Universe.

Electrons carry a negative charge and protons a positive one, and opposite charges attract while like charges push each other away. When you rub a balloon on your hair, some electrons move across from the hair to the balloon, and the two become oppositely charged, so the balloon clings to your head or to a wall. This is static electricity, and lightning is the same thing on a gigantic scale.

An electric current is a flow of electrons through a wire, rather like water running through a pipe. A battery acts as the pump, pushing the electrons round a complete circle, and as they pass through a bulb, a motor or a heater, they give up their energy. The electrons themselves drift very slowly, but the push travels almost at the speed of light, which is why a lamp lights the instant you flick the switch.

Every magnet has two poles, and the north pole of one magnet attracts the south pole of another. The Earth behaves like an enormous magnet, powered by the churning of the liquid iron deep in its core, and that is why a compass needle points towards the north. This magnetic field also deflects the stream of charged particles flowing from the Sun, and where they funnel down near the poles they make the glowing curtains of light called auroras.

In 1831 the English scientist Michael Faraday discovered that moving a magnet in and out of a coil of wire makes an electric current flow through it. The opposite is also true, because a current in a wire creates a magnetic force, and that is how electric motors work. Most of the electricity we use today is produced by generators, which are simply huge machines that keep magnets spinning near coils of wire.

In the 1860s the Scottish scientist James Clerk Maxwell wrote a set of equations that joined electricity and magnetism into a single theory. They predicted waves of electric and magnetic force travelling at exactly the speed of light, and Maxwell concluded that light itself must be such a wave. Twenty years later, Heinrich Hertz made the invisible waves we now call radio, and the modern age of communication began.

Light behaves like a wave in many experiments, yet in 1905 Albert Einstein showed that it also arrives in tiny packets of energy, which we now call photons. When photons strike certain metals they knock electrons loose, an effect that earned Einstein his Nobel Prize and that solar panels use to turn sunlight into electricity. Light is therefore both a wave and a stream of particles, which seems impossible until you remember that nature does not have to match our everyday pictures.

Electricity lights our homes, runs our computers and trains, and carries our voices and pictures around the world in an instant. About nine in every ten people alive today can now use it, which is a remarkable change, because two hundred years ago nobody could. All of this grew out of patient experiments with magnets, wires and sparks, which shows how curiosity can end up reshaping the world.

A famous story says that Isaac Newton watched an apple fall and began to wonder how far its pull might reach. He decided that the force dragging the apple to the ground, gravity, is the very same one that keeps the Moon circling the Earth, and that it grows weaker with distance in a regular way. This was a bold idea at the time, because it meant that the heavens obey the same laws as the ground beneath our feet.

At the height of the International Space Station, gravity is still about ninety per cent as strong as it is on the ground. Astronauts float because they and the station are in free fall, dropping towards the Earth while moving sideways so fast that they keep missing it. An orbit is therefore a kind of endless falling, and the Moon has been doing it for billions of years.

Gravity feels powerful, yet it is by far the weakest of the four basic forces of nature. A small fridge magnet can lift a paperclip against the pull of the entire Earth, which shows how much stronger electromagnetism is. Gravity matters on a large scale only because it always pulls and never cancels out, so the pulls of countless atoms add up to the force of a whole planet or star.

In 1915 Albert Einstein proposed a radically new picture of gravity, a theory known as general relativity. Mass and energy bend space and time together, he said, and objects simply follow the curves, rather as a marble rolls around the dent made by a heavy ball on a stretched sheet. The Moon circles the Earth not because it is pulled by a rope, but because it is following the straightest possible path through a curved space.

Einstein's theory made a bold prediction, that the light of a distant star passing close to the Sun should be bent by its gravity. The test had to wait for a total eclipse, when the sky goes dark enough to see stars beside the Sun, and in 1919 astronomers measured just such a shift. The news made Einstein famous around the world, and it showed that a good theory can be tested and supported by a simple observation.

According to Einstein, time itself runs a little more slowly where gravity is stronger, and very precise clocks have confirmed this, even over a difference in height of a few centimetres. The satellites of the Global Positioning System carry clocks that must be corrected for this effect and for their speed, or else the position shown on your phone would drift by several kilometres every day. Relativity is therefore not a distant curiosity but something you use whenever you find your way with a map on a screen.

Nothing that has mass can ever be pushed up to the speed of light, because the closer it gets, the more energy it needs. Einstein also showed that a fast-moving clock ticks more slowly than one that is standing still, an effect that has been measured with tiny particles and with atomic clocks carried around the world in aeroplanes. So the speed of light is not merely a limit on speed, but a basic rule that shapes how time and space fit together.

Einstein predicted in 1916 that violent events would send ripples through space and time, now known as gravitational waves. In 2015, almost a century later, two enormous detectors in the United States felt the faint tremble from two black holes that had spiralled together and merged more than a billion years earlier. It was a new way of observing the Universe, and it opened a window onto events that give out no light at all.

At the scale of atoms and smaller, nature follows strange rules that we call quantum physics, and they do not match everyday experience. Energy comes in tiny packets, particles can behave like waves, and we can never know both the exact position and the exact speed of a particle at the same moment. These ideas sound mad, but they have been tested thousands of times, and they have passed every test so far.

The rules of quantum physics explain how the transistors in a computer chip and the beam of a laser work, so they lie behind every phone, computer and hospital scanner. Yet they have never been joined smoothly to Einstein's picture of gravity, which describes the large scale, and physicists still do not know how the two fit together. A single theory that covers both would show how the Universe behaved at the very beginning, and it remains one of the great unsolved puzzles.

An adult brain weighs only about one and a half kilograms, roughly as much as a large bottle of water, yet it holds about eighty-six billion nerve cells. It makes up around two per cent of the body's weight but uses about a fifth of its energy, which shows how costly thinking is. It is often described as the most complex object that we know of anywhere in the Universe.

A nerve cell, called a neuron, has short branches that collect signals and a long fibre that sends them on. Inside the neuron a signal travels as a tiny electrical pulse, but between one neuron and the next it is carried across a minute gap, called a synapse, by chemical messengers. Your thoughts, feelings and movements are all patterns of such signals flickering through your brain.

Each neuron can connect to thousands of others, so that the brain contains at least a hundred trillion connections, far more than the number of stars in the Milky Way. What you know and remember is stored in the pattern of those connections, not in any single cell. That pattern is never quite the same from one day to the next, because every new experience reshapes it.

The lens of your eye focuses an upside-down image on the back of the eye, where cells turn light into electrical signals. Your brain interprets and combines those signals into the picture you see, and even colour is something that it creates from light of different wavelengths, since there is no colour in the waves themselves. Seeing is therefore not like looking through a window but more like watching a film that your brain is making all the time.

The wrinkled outer layer of the brain, called the cortex, is where most thinking, language and conscious sensation take place. Beneath it the cerebellum helps with balance and smooth movement, and the brainstem keeps essential things such as breathing and the heartbeat going without your attention. No single part works alone, however, and even a simple action such as catching a ball draws on many regions at once.

A seahorse-shaped region called the hippocampus helps the brain to form new memories, which are then stored in a spread-out pattern across many regions. Remembering is not like playing a recording, because each time you recall something your brain partly rebuilds it, and the rebuilt version can be altered by what you know now. This is why two honest people can remember the same event differently, and why forgetting is a normal part of how memory works.

When you learn something new, connections between neurons grow stronger, and every time you use that knowledge they strengthen further. In the 1880s the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus measured how fast we forget, and he found that memories fade quickly at first and then more slowly. Reviewing something just before it fades, and then again after longer gaps, is one of the most reliable ways to make it last, which is why language learners use spaced repetition.

During sleep the brain is far from switched off, and some parts are as active as when you are awake. Evidence suggests that it replays and sorts the learning of the day, strengthening the useful connections and tidying the rest.
