Most adults function best on about seven to nine hours of sleep a night, and tired brains find it harder to concentrate and to remember.

Children learn to speak simply by listening to the people around them, and by the age of five or so most of them have mastered the basic grammar of their language. Writing is only about five thousand years old, far too recent for evolution to have shaped a brain just for reading. Instead, reading borrows parts of the brain that evolved for seeing and for speech, and with practice they become wonderfully quick, which is exactly what happens when you read in a new language.

Scientists can now link many mental activities, such as seeing a face, feeling afraid or recalling a name, to particular patterns of activity in the brain. Yet how all that electrical and chemical activity becomes the inner experience of being you, which is called consciousness, remains one of the deepest unsolved puzzles. It is a strange and wonderful fact that the Universe has produced a brain able to wonder about itself.

Science begins with curiosity, when someone notices something odd and asks why it happens. The most useful questions are ones that can be tested, because they allow evidence rather than opinion to decide the answer. Almost every fact in this book began as a question that somebody was not willing to leave alone.

According to the story, about two thousand two hundred years ago the Greek scholar Eratosthenes heard that at noon on one day the Sun shone straight down a well in the city of Syene. In Alexandria, far to the north, a stick cast a short shadow at the same moment, and from the angle of that shadow and the distance between the cities he calculated the size of the whole Earth. His answer was remarkably close to the truth, although experts disagree about exactly how close, because we cannot be sure how long his unit of length was.

To test an idea, scientists form a hypothesis, which is a clear guess that evidence could prove wrong. Then they design a fair experiment that changes only one thing at a time and compares the result with a control, so that any difference can be traced to its cause. It is a simple habit of mind, and yet it separates real knowledge from lucky guesses.

For decades most doctors believed that stress and spicy food caused stomach ulcers, and the idea seemed reasonable and was widely taught. In the 1980s two Australian doctors showed that a bacterium lives in the stomach and is the real cause of many ulcers, and to prove their point one of them even drank a dish of the germs. Their evidence was strong enough to change the textbooks, and in 2005 they were awarded a Nobel Prize.

A good scientist tries as hard to prove her own ideas wrong as to prove them right. When the evidence disagrees with a favourite theory, the theory has to change or be abandoned, however much its author loved it. This is not a weakness of science but its greatest strength, because it means that mistakes are steadily found and removed.

In 2011 a team of scientists in Europe measured tiny particles that seemed to travel faster than light, which would have overturned Einstein's theory. Instead of announcing a revolution, they published their data openly and asked other scientists to find the mistake. Within months it was found, a loose cable in the timing equipment, and the speed limit of the Universe was safe once more.

Science is excellent at explaining how the world works, but questions about what is right, what is beautiful and what we ought to value need other kinds of thinking as well. It is also honest about its own limits, because when the evidence is not yet enough, the proper scientific answer is that we do not know. That answer is not a failure, but the place where the next discovery begins.

Many of the biggest questions remain open: what dark matter and dark energy really are, how life began, how a brain produces a mind, and how gravity can be joined with quantum physics. Each of them has occupied thousands of scientists for decades, and each may yet be answered by someone who is still at school. Perhaps one of those future scientists is reading this book at this very moment, wondering what to ask next.

Pause for a moment and consider what you are: atoms forged in stars that died long ago, arranged into cells that descend from the first living things, and organised into a brain that can ask how it all works. Every chapter of this book describes a step on the path that led to you. For nearly fourteen billion years the Universe has been changing, and one of the results is a creature able to understand some of it.

The atoms in your body were forged in stars, your cells descend from ancient life, and your brain is now able to ask how all of it works. Nothing you missed at school is lost, because the books are open and the questions are still waiting. Look up at the night sky, remember that you are part of this story, and never stop asking why.
